title: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
summary: How mobile and satellite networks are attacked and defended: SS7 and Diameter abuse, IMSI catchers, 5G identity and core security, SIM swaps, lawful-intercept targeting, cleartext GEO links, KA-SAT and GNSS spoofing.
outcomes: Explain why SS7 and Diameter let outsiders track phones and redirect SMS, and how category filtering and home routing stop it
Trace 3G/4G AKA and 5G SUCI concealment step by step and say what IMSI catchers and downgrades still exploit
Describe 5G core security: NRF OAuth tokens, SEPP checks on N32, and network slice authorisation
Treat SIM swaps, port-outs and eSIM activation as identity events, with carrier and relying-party controls
Explain how lawful-interception systems and carrier routers were abused (Athens, Salt Typhoon) and audit for it
Assess satellite links and GNSS timing: cleartext GEO backhaul, the KA-SAT attack, jamming and spoofing detection

lessons.title: How a mobile network fits together: radio, core and the HLR

blocks.md:
Every attack in this course targets one of a few boxes inside a mobile network, so we start by drawing them. Most of the rules come from **3GPP** (the 3rd Generation Partnership Project, the body that writes mobile standards; its specifications are published free by ETSI, the European Telecommunications Standards Institute). A tiny example: Ana, in London, texts Raj, whose phone is roaming in France. Ana's phone sends the text (an SMS, short message service message) by radio to a nearby mast. The operator's core network looks Raj up in a database, finds out which French network is serving Raj right now, and forwards the text across an operator-to-operator link to that network, which delivers it by radio.

That one text touched the radio network, two core networks, the link between operators and a subscriber database. Each is an attack surface, and each has its own defences.

The parts, with the names the standards use:

- **UE** (user equipment): the phone. Inside it, the **SIM** (subscriber identity module) or, from 3G on, the **USIM** (Universal SIM) holds the subscriber's secret key.
- **RAN** (radio access network): the base stations. Their names changed per generation: BTS (base transceiver station) in 2G, NodeB in 3G, eNodeB in 4G, gNB in 5G.
- **Core network**: switches and databases that route calls, texts and data.
- **HLR** (home location register), called **HSS** (home subscriber server) in 4G: in the words of [ENISA](https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/signalling-security-in-telecom-ss7-diameter-5g) (then the European Union Agency for Network and Information Security), a database holding each subscriber's profile, the shared secret also stored in their SIM, and transient data such as their current location.
- **VLR** (visitor location register), or **MME** (mobility management entity) in 4G: the serving network's local copy of the profiles of phones attached to it right now.

Two identifiers matter. The **IMSI** (international mobile subscriber identity) names the subscription inside networks. [3GPP TS 23.003](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/123000_123099/123003/19.08.00_60/ts_123003v190800p.pdf) defines it as at most 15 digits: a 3-digit **MCC** (mobile country code), a 2 or 3-digit **MNC** (mobile network code) that names the home network, and the **MSIN** (mobile subscriber identification number). The **MSISDN** (mobile station international subscriber directory number) is the phone number people dial. Knowing someone's phone number is easy; the IMSI is meant to stay inside the networks, and later lessons show why attackers work hard to get it.

**Roaming** is the reason operators must talk to each other. A French network has never seen Raj's SIM and does not hold Raj's key, so it asks Raj's home HLR for authentication data and the profile. ENISA notes operators connect either by direct bilateral links or through a carrier (an SS7 or IPX, Internetwork Packet Exchange, provider), and in the second case protection stops at each carrier's boundary.

blocks.title: One text to a roaming subscriber

scenes.caption: Raj's phone, in France, attaches by radio to a French base station, which hands it to the visited core (its VLR or MME).
The visited core has never seen this SIM and does not hold its key, so it asks Raj's home HLR/HSS, across the interconnect, for authentication data and the profile.
Once Raj is authenticated, the home HLR records which visited core is serving Raj. That location record is exactly what later attacks ask for.
Ana texts Raj. The home SMS centre asks the HLR where Raj is, then the text crosses the interconnect to the French core and goes out by radio.

blocks.code:
# Split an IMSI into its parts (3GPP TS 23.003) and build the Diameter home realm
THREE_DIGIT_MNC = {"310", "311", "312", "313", "316"}   # toy table: North American MCCs

def split_imsi(imsi: str):
    assert imsi.isdigit() and len(imsi) <= 15, "IMSI is at most 15 digits"
    mcc = imsi[:3]
    n = 3 if mcc in THREE_DIGIT_MNC else 2   # real code looks this up per network
    return mcc, imsi[3:3 + n], imsi[3 + n:]

def home_realm(mcc: str, mnc: str) -> str:
    return f"epc.mnc{mnc.zfill(3)}.mcc{mcc}.3gppnetwork.org"

for imsi in ["234150999999999", "310410123456789"]:
    mcc, mnc, msin = split_imsi(imsi)
    print(f"{imsi}: MCC={mcc} MNC={mnc} MSIN={msin}  realm={home_realm(mcc, mnc)}")
blocks.caption: Run with python3. The MNC length really depends on the country (TS 23.003); the toy table stands in for that lookup. The realm format epc.mnc<MNC>.mcc<MCC>.3gppnetwork.org is the 4G home network domain from TS 23.003, and its example (MCC 234, MNC 15) gives epc.mnc015.mcc234.3gppnetwork.org.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
234150999999999: MCC=234 MNC=15 MSIN=0999999999  realm=epc.mnc015.mcc234.3gppnetwork.org
310410123456789: MCC=310 MNC=410 MSIN=123456789  realm=epc.mnc410.mcc310.3gppnetwork.org
```

Notice what this means for a defender: the first digits of an IMSI say which network owns the subscriber. A firewall at the edge of your network can therefore ask "is this message about one of *our* subscribers, and is it coming from a network that may speak about them?". Lessons 4, 5 and 9 build exactly that check for three generations of signalling.

**Signalling versus user traffic.** Messages that set things up (attach, authenticate, update location, route a text) are **signalling**, also called the control plane. The calls, texts and data themselves are the user plane. Most telecom attacks in this course abuse signalling: the messages are legitimate in form, but sent by someone who should not be allowed to send them.

**Defender view.** The HLR/HSS is the crown jewel: it holds every subscriber's key and knows where everyone is. Protect who may query it (lessons 2 to 5 and 9), the secret it shares with the SIM (lessons 6 and 10), and the management systems around it (lessons 12 and 13).

The home HLR/HSS holds each subscriber's secret key and current location, and other networks must be able to query it for roaming to work. Mobile security is largely about who is allowed to ask it what.

blocks.question: A partner network sends your HLR a request about IMSI 234150999999999. Your network is MCC 234, MNC 15. What does the IMSI tell your HLR?
options: Nothing: an IMSI is just a random serial number
Which country the subscriber is in right now
That the subscriber is yours, because the MCC and MNC name your network as home
The subscriber's phone number
blocks.explain: The MCC and MNC at the start of an IMSI identify the home network (TS 23.003). They say nothing about where the phone is now (that is the HLR's location record), and the phone number is the separate MSISDN.

blocks.question: Why must a visited network contact the subscriber's home network when a roaming phone attaches?
options: Because only the home HLR/HSS holds the subscriber's key and profile, which the visited network needs to authenticate and serve the phone
To ask the home network to switch on the phone's radio
To download the phone's operating system updates
It does not: the visited network authenticates roaming phones by their phone number
blocks.explain: The shared secret lives only in the SIM and the home network (ENISA describes the HLR/HSS as holding it). The visited network gets authentication data and the profile from home, which is why operators must exchange signalling at all.

lessons.title: SS7: a signalling club that stopped being a club

blocks.md:
Imagine a phone exchange in 1980 that answers any question from another phone company: "where is this subscriber?", "send me their texts from now on". That was safe when only a few national operators could ask. The questions are still answered today; the club is no longer small.

**SS7** (Signalling System No. 7) is, in [ENISA](https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/signalling-security-in-telecom-ss7-diameter-5g)'s words, a set of signalling protocols developed in 1975, used between and within networks for call routing, roaming information and subscriber features. 2G and 3G networks rely on it, and **SIGTRAN** (signalling transport, an IETF protocol framework) carries it over IP. Three parts matter here:

- **MAP** (Mobile Application Part): the messages about subscribers and mobility (update location, send routing info, insert subscriber data).
- **SCCP** (Signalling Connection Control Part) routes messages using **Global Titles** (GTs), addresses for signalling nodes, roughly like IP addresses.
- **STPs** (signal transfer points) relay messages between networks, like routers.

**Why trust broke.** ENISA explains that the interconnect was built on trust between a small closed group of operators, with no real need for access control. Deregulation and market opening let many more parties in: virtual operators, bulk SMS firms, location services. ENISA notes SS7 access "can be easily purchased", and a [report](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/extcoop/figisymposium/Documents/ITU_SIT_WG_Technical%20report%20on%20the%20SS7%20vulnerabilities%20and%20their%20impact%20on%20DFS%20transactions_f.pdf) for the ITU (International Telecommunication Union, the UN agency for telecommunications) on SS7 and digital finance quotes dark-web offers of USD 150 to 2,500 for access.

The protocol itself does not help. ENISA's attack table says identifiers at various SS7 and Diameter levels "are not authenticated and may be spoofed". A message carries a sender GT, but nothing proves the sender owns it, and many attacks use only ordinary functions of the network. That is the core lesson: these are not bugs in one product, they are messages working as designed, accepted from someone who should not be sending them.

**Location tracking.** To deliver a text, a network must ask the recipient's HLR where they are, so the HLR answers. ITU's 2021 webinar deck by the security firm AdaptiveMobile ([slides](https://itu.int/en/ITU-T/webinars/dfs/sc/20211022/Documents/Session%232%20-Adaptive%20Mobile.pdf)) shows two routes: ask the HLR directly (AnyTimeInterrogation, which returns a cell ID), or indirectly: SendRoutingInfoForSM, meant for SMS delivery, returns the IMSI and the serving switch's address, and ProvideSubscriberInfo sent to that switch returns the cell. The cell ID names the mast serving the phone: what ENISA calls the subscriber's coarse location, and a prerequisite for further attacks.

**Interception.** UpdateLocation tells the HLR "this subscriber is now registered at my VLR". The ITU report describes it as an operation "causing the victim's home network to believe they have roamed to another network". If the HLR accepts it from an outsider, incoming texts are routed to the outsider. ENISA lists the effect plainly: SMS is used as a second factor, so attackers can intercept it to get around 2FA.

scenes.caption: Any node with interconnect access can send SendRoutingInfoForSM with Raj's phone number. This is the normal first step of delivering a text, so it is hard to block outright.
The HLR replies as it must for real SMS delivery: Raj's IMSI and the address of the switch serving Raj. The outsider now holds the internal identifier.
With the IMSI and switch address, a ProvideSubscriberInfo request asks the switch directly for Raj's cell. Nothing checks that the asker is Raj's home network.
Interception: an UpdateLocation claims Raj has moved to a VLR the outsider controls. Without filtering, the HLR records it.
Texts for Raj, including one-time codes, now go to the fake VLR. Raj's phone simply stops receiving texts, which few people notice quickly.

blocks.md: The common mistake is to look for a bug to patch. SS7 location tracking and SMS redirection use messages exactly as specified. The fix is deciding who may send which message about which subscriber, at the network edge.

**It happened in public.** In 2016 the US TV programme 60 Minutes showed researchers tracking and eavesdropping on US Representative Ted Lieu using only their phone number and SS7 access ([Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2017/05/thieves-drain-2fa-protected-bank-accounts-by-abusing-ss7-routing-protocol/)). In 2017, as the next lesson shows, criminals used the same weakness to empty bank accounts.

**Defender view.** *Prevent*: category filtering and SMS home routing at the edge (lesson 4). *Detect*: ENISA's survey of 39 EU operators (published March 2018) found that inspection at the STP or HLR was common, that 76% monitored the simplest message category but only about 43% the harder ones. *Respond*: operators "blacklist SCCP Global Titles" that emit malicious traffic (ENISA) and notify affected customers.

blocks.question: A location query about one of your subscribers arrives from a Global Title that belongs to a real foreign operator. Why is that not enough to trust it?
options: Global Titles are encrypted, so you cannot read them
Foreign operators are never allowed to send any SS7 message
Location queries are always sent by the subscriber's own phone
SS7 access is leased and resold, and SS7 identifiers are not authenticated, so a real operator's GT does not prove a legitimate sender or purpose
blocks.explain: ENISA notes SS7 access can be bought and that SS7 identifiers can be spoofed. Foreign operators do legitimately send many messages (roaming needs them), so a blanket ban is wrong; the question is whether this message type, about this subscriber, makes sense from that source.

blocks.question: After a successful fake UpdateLocation, what is the most likely thing the victim notices?
options: Their phone shows a security warning
Incoming texts stop arriving, while the phone otherwise seems normal
Their battery drains quickly
Their phone number changes
blocks.explain: The attack changes where the home network sends traffic for the subscriber; it does not touch the phone. The ITU report notes that when an UpdateLocation is used to cut someone off, the victim placing a call or sending a text reverses the effect almost immediately. (Our inference: redirection is most useful briefly, around the moment a one-time code is sent.)

lessons.title: Case: SMS codes rerouted to drain German bank accounts (2017)

blocks.md:
In 2017 the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung reported that criminals had emptied German bank accounts by redirecting their victims' text messages over SS7. [Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2017/05/thieves-drain-2fa-protected-bank-accounts-by-abusing-ss7-routing-protocol/) summarised the report. The banks used **mTANs** (mobile transaction authentication numbers): one-time codes sent by SMS to approve a transfer. Online banking needed a password to log in and an mTAN to move money.

The attackers needed both factors, and they got them from two different weaknesses:

1. **The password**: traditional banking trojans (malware) on the victims' computers stole their online banking passwords. With those, the attackers could log in and see balances, but not move money.
2. **The code**: the attackers redirected the victims' incoming texts so that the mTANs went to numbers they controlled, then used them to transfer money out.

blocks.title: Two factors, two separate weaknesses (order only, not to scale)

scenes.caption: Step 1: a banking trojan on the victim's computer steals the online banking password. The attackers can now log in and see the balance, but transfers need an mTAN.
Step 2: over SS7, the victim's incoming texts are redirected to the attackers. O2 Telefonica said the attack came from a foreign operator's network.
Step 3: the attackers start a transfer, the bank sends the mTAN by SMS, and it arrives at the attackers instead of the victim, whose phone receives nothing.
Response: the operator blocked the foreign network the attack came from and informed affected customers. Blocking one source stops one campaign, not the class of attack.

blocks.md:
O2 Telefónica, a German operator, confirmed it: "Criminals carried out an attack from a network of a foreign mobile network operator in the middle of January ... The attack redirected incoming SMS messages for selected German customers to the attackers." The foreign provider was blocked and affected customers were informed. ENISA's 2018 report lists the same case among confirmed signalling attacks.

Ars points out why SS7 appealed to the criminals: the older way to get someone's mTANs was a duplicate SIM card (a SIM swap, lesson 11), obtained one victim at a time; SS7 compromises "can be done remotely on a much larger quantity of phone numbers".

Neither factor was broken alone. The password fell to malware on the PC; the SMS code fell to the phone network. Two factors only help when they fail independently, and an SMS code depends on a network the bank does not control.

**What a bank can do**, from the [ITU report](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/extcoop/figisymposium/Documents/ITU_SIT_WG_Technical%20report%20on%20the%20SS7%20vulnerabilities%20and%20their%20impact%20on%20DFS%20transactions_f.pdf) on digital finance, which lists mitigations that need no help from the operator:
- Stop relying on SMS: use an app-based or out-of-band method outside the telecom ecosystem where customers have smartphones.
- Before approving, check telecom signals: has the IMSI behind the number changed (a sign of SIM swap), does the phone's network location make sense.
- Make SMS flows bidirectional where SMS must stay: show a code on screen and ask the user to send it *from* their phone, so the reply's network origin can be checked.

The 2026 ITU follow-up ([DFS-SS7-2026](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/dfs/seclab/PublishingImages/Pages/default/Recommendations%20to%20mitigate%20Signalling%20System%20No.%207%20vulnerabilities%20in%20digital%20financial%20services.pdf)) adds a caution: signalling-derived data such as location, IMSI or SMS delivery "must not be the sole basis for authentication decisions" and must be combined with additional authentication factors.

blocks.prompt: Suppose the bank had used codes from an authenticator app (TOTP, from the prerequisite course) instead of SMS. Which part of the 2017 attack fails, and is the account now safe?
blocks.reveal: The SS7 step fails: there is no SMS to redirect, and the code is computed on the phone from a shared secret. But the account is not fully safe. The attackers still had malware on the victim's PC, and a TOTP code can be phished or relayed in real time (prerequisite lesson "Real-time phishing proxies and help-desk social engineering"). Phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys bind the login to the bank's real site, which also defeats the relay. Fixing one channel moves the attacker to the next weakest one.

blocks.question: In the 2017 German case, who was best placed to stop the SMS redirection itself?
options: The victims, by installing antivirus on their phones
The mobile operators, by filtering signalling messages at their network edge
The banks, by encrypting their text messages
The newspaper that reported it
blocks.explain: SS7 messages travel between operators' core networks; ENISA stresses that subscribers can do very little and that most protection must be done by providers. Phone antivirus cannot see core signalling, and SMS cannot be end-to-end encrypted by the bank. Banks can reduce their reliance on SMS, but only the operator can stop the redirection.

lessons.title: Signalling firewalls: message categories, home routing, monitoring

blocks.md:
A firewall for IP traffic asks "which address and port?". A signalling firewall asks a richer question: "is this message type, about this subscriber, plausible from this network, given where the subscriber was a minute ago?". Tiny example: a request for one of your subscribers' location arrives from a network on another continent while your HLR knows the subscriber is at home. No legitimate roaming flow produces that.

The industry body for mobile operators, the **GSMA** (originally the GSM Association; GSM, the Global System for Mobile Communications, is the 2G standard), wrote the rulebooks: **FS.11** (SS7 interconnect security monitoring and firewall guidelines), FS.07 (SS7 and SIGTRAN security), **FS.19** (Diameter), FS.20 (GTP) and others. They are restricted to members; the [ITU report](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/extcoop/figisymposium/Documents/ITU_SIT_WG_Technical%20report%20on%20the%20SS7%20vulnerabilities%20and%20their%20impact%20on%20DFS%20transactions_f.pdf) notes this and ENISA says GSMA opened access to regulators. So this lesson works from public descriptions of them.

Public material, such as ITU's 2021 webinar deck by AdaptiveMobile ([slides](https://itu.int/en/ITU-T/webinars/dfs/sc/20211022/Documents/Session%232%20-Adaptive%20Mobile.pdf)), describes three FS.11 categories of MAP messages:

- **Category 1**: should normally never be exchanged between operators (intra-network only). Examples: SendIMSI, SendRoutingInfo, SendRoutingInfoForLCS, AnyTimeInterrogation. Rule: block at the edge.
- **Category 2**: must cross between operators, but only the subscriber's **home** network may send them. Examples: ProvideSubscriberInfo, InsertSubscriberData, ProvideRoamingNumber. Rule: the sender's GT must belong to the network that owns the IMSI.
- **Category 3**: must come from the network the subscriber is **visiting**. Examples: UpdateLocation, UpdateGPRSLocation, SendAuthenticationInfo. Rule: "trajectory plausibility" (could they have travelled there that fast?); category 3.1 messages such as MO-Forward-SM get "network memory" (right country?).

The deck adds a caution: messages "do not always strictly fit into a single Category".

blocks.caption: A toy, not a product: real firewalls decode SCCP and TCAP (transaction capabilities application part, the layer that carries MAP operations), keep state per subscriber, handle many more message types and use real geography. Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
AnyTimeInterrogation  from 99901: block cat1: never valid between networks
ProvideSubscriberInfo from 99901: block cat2: only the subscriber's home may send it
ProvideSubscriberInfo from 20801: allow
UpdateLocation        from 99901: block cat3: implies 19,508 km/h
UpdateLocation        from 20801: allow
```

The third line is a French network asking about its *own* subscriber roaming in our network: legitimate. The fourth claims our London subscriber registered near Jakarta 30 minutes later. The fifth, a Paris registration three hours later, is plausible. Note the blocked registration did not update `last`: a firewall must never let a rejected message move its own memory.

blocks.title: The rule engine, one message at a time

scenes.caption: AnyTimeInterrogation is category 1: it should never arrive from another network at all, whoever it is about. Blocked on type alone.
ProvideSubscriberInfo is category 2. It is about our subscriber, but it comes from network 99901, which is not that subscriber's home. Blocked.
The same message type from 20801 about 20801's own subscriber, who is roaming here, is how roaming is supposed to work. Allowed.
UpdateLocation is category 3. Our subscriber was in London half an hour ago; a registration near Jakarta implies about 19,500 km/h. Blocked, and memory is not updated.
A Paris registration three hours after London is plausible travel. Allowed, and the firewall now expects the subscriber in France.

blocks.md:
**SMS home routing.** Category 3 attacks need the victim's IMSI, so the deck calls preventing IMSI leaks "the most important line of defense". The classic leak is SendRoutingInfoForSM (lesson 2), which must be answered for texts to work. With home routing, an SMS router in the home network answers instead, so foreign senders no longer receive the real IMSI and switch address in every inbound SMS flow. The ITU report adds that the IMSI may still leak through other signalling, so home routing complements filtering rather than replacing it.

**Adoption.** ENISA's survey of 39 EU operators found 87% used SMS home routing, 71% filtered on transit and end nodes, and only about 28% ran a dedicated signalling firewall. Three quarters named cost and complexity as the brake.

**What goes wrong.**

- *False positives.* ENISA notes tracking detection is "more subject to false positives than any other type", mostly from misconfiguration, and that blocking a legitimate message can carry liability.
- *Border cases.* The deck's example: a subscriber can cross into a neighbouring country within minutes, so trajectory rules need real geography and tolerances.
- *Inbound roamers.* Category 2 checks are usually enforced only for your own IMSIs, so visitors roaming in your network are less protected (deck).
- *One protocol at a time.* The 2026 ITU report ([DFS-SS7-2026](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/dfs/seclab/PublishingImages/Pages/default/Recommendations%20to%20mitigate%20Signalling%20System%20No.%207%20vulnerabilities%20in%20digital%20financial%20services.pdf)) asks for rate limiting, anomaly detection on volume and origin, and cross-protocol consistency checks across SS7, Diameter and SIP.

Signalling firewalls apply three ideas: some messages never belong on the interconnect, some may only come from the subscriber's home, and some must match where the subscriber actually is. Hiding the IMSI (home routing) makes the third kind much harder to abuse.

blocks.question: A message type that only the subscriber's home network should send about that subscriber arrives from a network that does not own the IMSI. Which category rule catches it?
options: Category 1: block the message type everywhere
Category 3: check trajectory plausibility
None: home routing handles it
Category 2: check the sender against the IMSI's home network
blocks.explain: That is the definition of category 2: legitimate between operators, but only from the subscriber's home. Blocking the type everywhere would break roaming, and trajectory checks apply to messages from the visited network.

blocks.question: Why does hiding the real IMSI in SMS delivery (home routing) reduce category 3 attacks such as fake UpdateLocation?
options: Category 3 messages are addressed by IMSI, so an attacker who only knows the phone number cannot target them
It encrypts all SS7 messages
It blocks all foreign UpdateLocation messages
It makes the HLR reject every message from abroad
blocks.explain: The deck notes category 3 attacks are only possible if the IMSI is known. SendRoutingInfoForSM was the easy way to turn a phone number into an IMSI; home routing closes that route, though not every route, so filtering is still needed.

lessons.title: Diameter in 4G roaming: the same trust model on IP

blocks.md:
4G replaced SS7 between core networks with **Diameter**, an authentication, authorisation and accounting protocol derived from RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service), as [ENISA](https://www.enisa.europa.eu/publications/signalling-security-in-telecom-ss7-diameter-5g) describes it. The HLR became the HSS and the VLR became the MME. In the roaming procedures of [TS 29.272](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/129200_129299/129272/19.06.00_60/ts_129272v190600p.pdf), the visited MME sends an Update-Location-Request (ULR) to tell the home HSS it now serves the user, and the HSS sends Insert-Subscriber-Data-Requests (IDR) to whichever MME serves its user.

Each Diameter message carries **AVPs** (attribute-value pairs). [RFC 6733](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6733) requires every message to carry **Origin-Host** and **Origin-Realm**, naming the sender. A **realm** is a domain name; for 4G home networks, TS 23.003 fixes it as `epc.mnc<MNC>.mcc<MCC>.3gppnetwork.org`. Messages travel through **IPX** (Internetwork Packet Exchange) carriers and Diameter relay agents.

ENISA's verdict: Diameter "has borrowed many concepts from SS7, along with its vulnerabilities", and being purely IP-based it may be simpler to exploit. Nothing in a plain Diameter message proves that the sender owns the Origin-Realm it claims.

blocks.title: A 4G roaming request, a spoofed one, and the edge check

scenes.caption: Legitimate: our subscriber roams in network 208-01. Its MME sends an Update-Location-Request with Origin-Realm epc.mnc001.mcc208..., through the IPX, to our HSS.
Spoofed: a sender with leased interconnect access sends Insert-Subscriber-Data about our own subscriber, claiming the partner's realm. Only our HSS ever sends that about our users.
The edge applies a category 2 style rule: only the subscriber's home realm sends Insert-Subscriber-Data about them. Our own IMSI from a foreign realm: rejected before it reaches our nodes.

blocks.code:
# Toy Diameter edge check: does the claimed sender match the subscriber?
# Realm format from 3GPP TS 23.003: epc.mnc<MNC>.mcc<MCC>.3gppnetwork.org
OUR_REALM = "epc.mnc015.mcc234.3gppnetwork.org"
PEERS = {"epc.mnc001.mcc208.3gppnetwork.org"}        # roaming agreements

def realm_of(imsi, mnc_len=2):
    return f"epc.mnc{imsi[3:3+mnc_len].zfill(3)}.mcc{imsi[:3]}.3gppnetwork.org"

def edge_check(req):
    o, imsi, cmd = req["Origin-Realm"], req["User-Name"], req["cmd"]
    if o not in PEERS:
        return "reject: no roaming agreement"
    if cmd == "Insert-Subscriber-Data" and realm_of(imsi) != o:
        return "reject: only the subscriber's home realm sends IDR"
    if cmd == "Update-Location" and realm_of(imsi) != OUR_REALM:
        return "reject: ULR for someone else's subscriber"
    return "accept"

reqs = [
  {"cmd": "Update-Location", "Origin-Realm": "epc.mnc001.mcc208.3gppnetwork.org",
   "User-Name": "234150000000001"},                    # our user roaming in 208-01
  {"cmd": "Insert-Subscriber-Data", "Origin-Realm": "epc.mnc001.mcc208.3gppnetwork.org",
   "User-Name": "234150000000001"},                    # peer edits OUR user's profile
  {"cmd": "Update-Location", "Origin-Realm": "epc.mnc099.mcc999.3gppnetwork.org",
   "User-Name": "234150000000001"},                    # unknown network
]
for r in reqs:

```

Update-Location        from mnc099.mcc999: reject: no roaming agreement
```

**The limit of this check**: it trusts the Origin-Realm field, which the sender writes. A real edge must also bind the claimed realm to *how the message arrived*: which IPX connection, which authenticated peer. That cross-layer idea returns in 5G, where the SEPP must verify that the sending peer is authorised for the network ID it claims (lesson 9).

**Adoption lags.** ENISA found Diameter security less mature than SS7's: 60% of surveyed operators inspected Diameter interconnect traffic fully or partially, many did not monitor it at all, and "attacks spoofing application ID are likely to work in most cases". At the time no respondent reported seeing real Diameter attacks, which ENISA attributed partly to attackers still finding SS7 easier. The ITU deck also lists a **low layer** threat category next to categories 1 to 3: malformed messages and protocol abuse aimed at the receiving node itself.

**GTP** (GPRS Tunnelling Protocol; GPRS is General Packet Radio Service, packet data for GSM) is the third interconnect protocol: it carries roaming users' data sessions. ENISA found 53% of respondents monitored its control messages (GTP-C). GSMA FS.20 covers GTP filtering.

Moving from SS7 to Diameter, or to any IP protocol, does not add authentication by itself. If the edge does not check which peer may speak for which subscribers, the new protocol inherits the old trust model.

blocks.question: Your edge sees an Update-Location-Request about IMSI 208010000000042 arriving from a partner realm. Your network is 234-15. What should a category-style rule conclude?
options: Accept: ULRs from partners are always fine
Accept, but only if the subscriber is a VIP
Reject: your HSS is not that subscriber's home, so a ULR for them should not be sent to you
Reject: ULRs are category 1 and never cross networks
blocks.explain: A visited MME sends Update-Location to the subscriber's home HSS. IMSI 20801... belongs to network 208-01, not you, so a ULR for it addressed to your HSS has no legitimate purpose. ULRs do cross networks, so they are not category 1.

blocks.question: Why is checking Origin-Realm alone not enough?
options: Origin-Realm is encrypted and cannot be read
Origin-Realm only exists in SS7
Realms change every hour
Origin-Realm is written by the sender, so it must be bound to the authenticated peer or connection the message actually came from
blocks.explain: The field is a claim. Without binding it to the transport peer, a rogue sender with interconnect access simply writes a partner's realm. 5G makes this binding explicit at the SEPP.

lessons.title: Who proves what on the radio: GSM one-way, 3G and 4G mutual

blocks.md:
**AKA** (Authentication and Key Agreement), specified in [TS 33.102](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133100_133199/133102/19.01.00_60/ts_133102v190100p.pdf), clause 6.3, fixes the one-way problem. The USIM and the home **AuC** (authentication centre) share a secret key K and keep sequence numbers: SQN_MS in the USIM, SQN_HE at home.

1. Home makes an authentication vector: a random challenge RAND, the expected response XRES, cipher and integrity keys CK and IK, and an authentication token AUTN.
2. The serving network sends RAND and AUTN to the phone.
3. The USIM computes the anonymity key AK, recovers SQN, recomputes the MAC and compares it with the one in AUTN. A wrong MAC means the network does not know K: reject.
4. It checks SQN is fresh: an old vector is rejected.
5. Only then does it return RES; the network compares RES with XRES.

So the phone authenticates the network (steps 3 and 4) and the network authenticates the phone (step 5). TS 33.102 calls this mutual authentication, and 4G and 5G AKA keep the same core.

blocks.caption: From TS 33.102. AMF here is the authentication management field. XOR with AK hides SQN, which could otherwise reveal identity and location. The operator chooses the algorithm set; 3GPP publishes example sets such as MILENAGE.

blocks.code:
# Toy AKA (shape of TS 33.102 6.3). HMAC stands in for MILENAGE f1, f2, f5.
import hmac, hashlib
def f(K, tag, data, n=8): return hmac.new(K, tag + data, hashlib.sha256).digest()[:n]
def xor(a, b): return bytes(x ^ y for x, y in zip(a, b))
AMF = b"\x80\x00"

def home_make_vector(K, sqn, rand):                # runs in the home AuC
    s = sqn.to_bytes(6, "big")
    mac = f(K, b"f1", s + rand + AMF)
    autn = xor(s, f(K, b"f5", rand, 6)) + AMF + mac
    return rand, autn, f(K, b"f2", rand)           # RAND, AUTN, XRES

class USIM:
    def __init__(self, K): self.K, self.sqn_ms = K, 0
    def answer(self, rand, autn):
        s = xor(autn[:6], f(self.K, b"f5", rand, 6))  # undo the anonymity key
        xmac = f(self.K, b"f1", s + rand + autn[6:8])
        if not hmac.compare_digest(xmac, autn[8:]):
            return "reject: MAC fails, network does not know K"
        sqn = int.from_bytes(s, "big")
        if sqn <= self.sqn_ms:
            return "reject: SQN not fresh (replayed vector)"
        self.sqn_ms = sqn
        return "RES=" + f(self.K, b"f2", rand).hex()

K = bytes(range(16))                               # fixed demo key
sim = USIM(K)
rand, autn, xres = home_make_vector(K, 1, b"R" * 16)
print("real network :", sim.answer(rand, autn), "| XRES=" + xres.hex())
print("replay       :", sim.answer(rand, autn))
print("fake network :", sim.answer(b"F" * 16, b"X" * 16))

blocks.md:
**What AKA does not fix.** AKA runs *after* the phone has said who it is, and some messages are exchanged before any keys exist. When a network cannot recognise a phone's temporary identity, it may send an Identity Request, and before 5G the phone answered with its IMSI in clear (5G changes this, lesson 8). And none of this helps if the phone can be talked down to 2G, where network authentication does not exist. Those two gaps are what IMSI catchers use.

**Defender view.** AKA moves trust into two places: the secrecy of K (the SIM and the AuC, lesson 10) and the integrity of the home network that issues vectors. Protect the AuC/HSS like a key-management system; TS 33.120 lists authentication data sent in clear between networks as a GSM weakness to avoid.

blocks.question: A false base station recorded yesterday's RAND and AUTN from a real network and replays them to your phone today. What stops it?
options: The sequence number check: SQN is not higher than the last one the USIM accepted
The MAC check, because the MAC changes every day
Nothing: replayed vectors always work
The phone checks the base station's GPS position
blocks.explain: The MAC is valid (it was made by the real home network), so step 3 passes. Freshness comes from SQN: the USIM only accepts a sequence number above the highest it has seen, as in the trace.

blocks.question: According to TS 33.120, which of these was a design weakness of GSM security?
options: SIM cards had no secret key
The network was never authenticated to the phone, so active attacks with a false base station were possible
Calls were encrypted end to end between handsets, which blocked lawful interception
GSM required a password for every call
blocks.explain: TS 33.120 lists false-BTS attacks as the first weakness to fix in 3G. GSM SIMs did hold a key (for one-way authentication), and encryption stopped at the base station rather than being end to end.

lessons.title: IMSI catchers and false base stations: downgrade and detection

blocks.md:
A phone picks a mast by signal strength and the broadcast information the mast sends. Google's Android security team put the problem simply in 2023: "a smartphone cannot reliably know the legitimacy of the cellular base station before attempting to connect to it" ([Android 14 announcement](https://security.googleblog.com/2023/08/android-14-introduces-first-of-its-kind.html)). A **false base station** (FBS) is a radio transmitter that pretends to be a network's mast. An **IMSI catcher** is a false base station used to collect the permanent identities of phones nearby; Google's post also uses "Stingrays" for such surveillance devices.

What they exploit is the previous lesson's two gaps:

1. **Identity before security.** Before 5G, a phone that was asked for its identity before any keys existed answered with the IMSI in clear. The [ITU report](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/extcoop/figisymposium/Documents/ITU_SIT_WG_Technical%20report%20on%20the%20SS7%20vulnerabilities%20and%20their%20impact%20on%20DFS%20transactions_f.pdf) lists "IMSI catching (of all phones in the vicinity)" as an information-gathering step.
2. **Downgrade.** Android's team writes that devices can be silently downgraded from 5G and 4G to 2G, where GSM's lack of mutual authentication "enables trivial Person-in-the-Middle attacks", and that this is "the most common use of FBSs, IMSI catchers and Stingrays".

blocks.title: What a false base station relies on (conceptual)

scenes.caption: The false station broadcasts as a strong cell of the victim's network. The phone has no way to verify a mast before connecting, so it starts a normal procedure.
Before any keys exist, the station asks who the phone is. On 2G, 3G and 4G the phone could answer with its IMSI in clear: the 'catch'.
Interception needs more: the station pushes the phone towards 2G, where the network is never authenticated. It cannot pass the 3G/4G AKA check of the last lesson.

Defence on the phone: with 2G disabled at the modem (Android 12 onward) there is no unauthenticated network to fall back to. A false 4G cell can still ask for the IMSI; only on 5G is the identity concealed.

blocks.md:
**Research shows 4G has gaps too.** Altaf Shaik, Ravishankar Borgaonkar and colleagues analysed LTE (Long Term Evolution, the 4G standard) access protocols in 2016 ([abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.07563)). Using commercial phones in real networks they showed "inexpensive, and practical attacks": three ways to make a device leak its location, from a coarse area of a city to precise coordinates, and attacks that "persistently deny some or all services". Their point: LTE was "considered to be significantly better than its predecessors" for security and privacy, yet its access-network protocols still had practical weaknesses.

**Null ciphers.** Even on a genuine network, the network chooses whether to encrypt the radio link. Android 14 added a switch to refuse **null-ciphered** connections (no encryption), because Google noted "recent reports identified usage of null ciphers in commercial networks", exposing voice and SMS, including one-time passwords.

**Defences, by who owns them.**

- *Phone users and fleets:* Android 12 added a modem-level switch to disable 2G (Pixel 6 first). Android 14 lets organisations using Android Enterprise block 2G on managed devices and adds the null-cipher setting. Emergency calls keep working.
- *Operators:* turn 2G off (Google notes most major US carriers have), and detect false stations from the network side. TS 33.501 Annex E describes using phones' **measurement reports** (the signal strength, cell ID and frequency they see) to spot cells with an unknown ID, an unplanned frequency, or a signal far stronger than planning predicts. Reports from many phones filter out a single lying one.
- *Regulators:* the ITU report suggests continuous testing with operators to detect IMSI catchers.

blocks.caption: Toy network-side detector in the spirit of TS 33.501 Annex E, on synthetic reports. Real systems use radio planning data, location and many more reports. Run with python3.

Output:

```
cell 1101: signal 20+ dB stronger than planned; 2 UE(s), ALERT
cell 1102: signal 20+ dB stronger than planned; 1 UE(s), watch (single UE, could be a rogue report)
cell 1201: cell on a channel we never configured; 2 UE(s), ALERT
cell 1999: cell id not in our deployment; 2 UE(s), ALERT
```

Cell 1101 is a real cell ID: a false station copying a genuine cell's identity is caught only by the power anomaly. Requiring two independent phones before alerting keeps one faulty or malicious phone from triggering a response.
Turning on 5G does not remove the 2G risk by itself. As long as the phone will still accept 2G, an attacker can try to push it there. Disabling 2G on the device is what closes the fallback.

blocks.question: Why can a false base station not simply impersonate a 4G network all the way through to intercepting calls?
options: 4G masts have unique colours that phones check
4G phones never send any messages before authentication
4G AKA makes the phone verify a MAC that only the home network (which knows K) can produce, so the false station pushes the phone to 2G instead
4G uses satellites instead of masts
blocks.explain: AKA authenticates the network to the phone, so a false 4G station cannot complete authentication. That is why downgrade to 2G, where the network is never authenticated, is the common route. Some messages are still exchanged before authentication in 4G, which Shaik et al. exploited for location leaks and denial of service.

blocks.question: In the detector, cell 1102 has one report 40 dB too strong. Why is it only on 'watch'?
options: Because 40 dB is a normal variation
Because cell 1102 is not in the deployment
Because a single report could come from a faulty or malicious phone; Annex E suggests using reports from several phones to filter incorrect ones
Because the frequency is wrong
blocks.explain: One phone's report is weak evidence. TS 33.501 Annex E notes measurement reports collected from multiple UEs can filter out incorrect reports from a potential rogue UE.

lessons.title: 5G identity privacy: SUPI, SUCI and ECIES concealment

blocks.md:
5G stops the phone from ever sending its permanent identity in clear. Tiny example: a phone whose IMSI is home network 274-012 plus MSIN 001002086 registers (the test subscriber in TS 33.501 Annex C). Instead of sending 001002086, it sends 45 bytes that look random and differ every time, plus the readable network code 274-012 so the visited network knows where to forward them.

The names, from [TS 33.501](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133500_133599/133501/19.07.00_60/ts_133501v190700p.pdf), clause 6.12:

- **SUPI** (subscription permanent identifier): the permanent identity, for example one containing the IMSI.
- **SUCI** (subscription concealed identifier): the SUPI with its subscriber part encrypted under the **home network's public key**. The MCC, MNC and routing indicator stay in clear so the request can be routed home.
- **SIDF** (subscription identifier de-concealing function): in the home **UDM** (unified data management), the only place holding the private key.
- **5G-GUTI** (globally unique temporary UE identity): the temporary identity used after registration, which the network must refresh, for example after paging.

The spec is blunt: "In response to the Identity Request message, the UE never sends the SUPI."

blocks.title: What a SUCI contains (IMSI-based, Profile A)

scenes.caption: Everything except the scheme output is in clear: the visited network must read the home network code and routing indicator to forward the SUCI. Values are illustrative.
Scheme 0x1 is ECIES Profile A. The output is the UE's fresh ephemeral public key (32 bytes), the encrypted MSIN (5 bytes here) and an 8-byte MAC tag.
With scheme 0x0, the null-scheme, the 'output' is the MSIN itself. The SUCI then conceals nothing: the spec says the null-scheme provides no privacy protection.

blocks.md:
**ECIES** (Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme) combines a key agreement with symmetric encryption and a MAC. Annex C of TS 33.501 fixes two profiles that every phone and SIDF must implement:

- **Profile A**: Curve25519 with X25519 key agreement, the ANSI X9.63 KDF with SHA-256, AES-128 in counter mode, HMAC-SHA-256 truncated to 8 bytes.
- **Profile B**: the NIST P-256 curve (secp256r1) with point compression, otherwise the same.

The phone makes a fresh ephemeral key pair for every SUCI, agrees a shared secret with the home public key, derives 64 bytes (16 encryption key, 16 counter block, 32 MAC key) and outputs ephemeral public key, ciphertext and tag. The MSIN is first packed as BCD (binary-coded decimal) digits. The code below reproduces the spec's own test vector.

blocks.code:
# SUCI, ECIES Profile A (TS 33.501 Annex C), checked against test data C.4.3.1
import hashlib, hmac
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.x25519 import X25519PrivateKey as Priv, X25519PublicKey as Pub
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes

def kdf(z, info, n):   # ANSI X9.63 KDF, SHA-256
    out, c = b"", 1
    while len(out) < n:
        out += hashlib.sha256(z + c.to_bytes(4, "big") + info).digest(); c += 1
    return out[:n]

def bcd(msin):   # packed BCD, low nibble first
    d = msin + "F" * (len(msin) % 2)
    return bytes(int(d[i+1], 16) << 4 | int(d[i], 16) for i in range(0, len(d), 2))

def conceal(msin, hn_pub, eph):
    eph_pub = eph.public_key().public_bytes_raw()
    k = kdf(eph.exchange(Pub.from_public_bytes(hn_pub)), eph_pub, 64)
    ek, icb, mk = k[:16], k[16:32], k[32:]
    e = Cipher(algorithms.AES(ek), modes.CTR(icb)).encryptor()
    ct = e.update(bcd(msin)) + e.finalize()
    return eph_pub + ct + hmac.new(mk, ct, hashlib.sha256).digest()[:8]

hn = bytes.fromhex("5a8d38864820197c3394b92613b20b91633cbd897119273bf8e4a6f4eec0a650")
eph = Priv.from_private_bytes(bytes.fromhex(
      "c80949f13ebe61af4ebdbd293ea4f942696b9e815d7e8f0096bbf6ed7de62256"))
out = conceal("001002086", hn, eph)
print("BCD input :", bcd("001002086").hex())
print("ciphertext:", out[32:-8].hex(), "| MAC:", out[-8:].hex())
print("matches spec:", out.hex().endswith("cb02352410cddd9e730ef3fa87"))
a, b = (conceal("001002086", hn, Priv.generate()) for _ in range(2))
print("two fresh SUCIs equal?", a == b, "| bytes:", len(a))
blocks.caption: Needs the cryptography package: python3 -m venv venv, then venv/bin/pip install cryptography. The keys are the published test data from TS 33.501 C.4.3.1, never real keys.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
BCD input : 00012080f6
ciphertext: cb02352410 | MAC: cddd9e730ef3fa87
matches spec: True
two fresh SUCIs equal? False | bytes: 45
```

Two SUCIs for the same subscriber differ because each uses a new ephemeral key, so a listener cannot link them. The size matches Annex C: a 256-bit public key, a 64-bit MAC, plus the input.

**When SUCI protects nothing.** The phone must use the null-scheme for an unauthenticated emergency session without a 5G-GUTI, if the home network configured null-scheme, or if the home network did not provision a public key in the USIM. An operator that skips provisioning ships 5G with 4G-level identity privacy.

**Formal analysis found gaps.** Researchers David Basin and colleagues built the first comprehensive formal model of 5G AKA and checked it with Tamarin, a security protocol verification tool (2018, [abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/1806.10360)) and found "some critical security goals are not met, except under additional assumptions missing from the standard", with proposed fixes. And SUCI does nothing if the phone is pushed down to 4G or 2G (lesson 7).

**Long-lived keys and quantum computers.** The home network key pair lives for years in USIMs. Annex C caps proprietary scheme outputs at 3000 octets plus input precisely "to allow the introduction of quantum-resistant protection schemes"; [NIST IR 8547](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/ir/8547/final) deprecates elliptic-curve schemes after 2030 and disallows them after 2035, so plan a migration path.

SUCI encrypts the subscriber part of the identity under the home network's public key with a fresh ephemeral key each time, so listeners can neither read nor link it. It only works if the operator provisions the key and the phone cannot be downgraded.

blocks.question: An operator launches 5G but never provisions the home network public key in its USIMs. What does a 5G phone on that network send when asked for its identity?
options: A SUCI using the null-scheme, which contains the MSIN in clear
A SUCI encrypted with a default public key
Nothing: the phone refuses to register
Its 5G-GUTI, which the network can always resolve
blocks.explain: TS 33.501 says the phone uses the null-scheme if the home network has not provisioned the public key. The null-scheme returns the input unchanged, so the identity is effectively in clear.

blocks.question: Why do two SUCIs for the same subscriber, generated a second apart, look completely different?
options: The MSIN changes every second
The home network rotates its private key every second
The phone adds a timestamp to the MSIN
Each SUCI uses a fresh ephemeral key pair, so the shared secret, keys and ciphertext all change
blocks.explain: ECIES generates a new ephemeral key pair per encryption. That gives unlinkability: a passive listener cannot tell that two SUCIs belong to the same person.

lessons.title: Inside the 5G core: service APIs, OAuth tokens, SEPP and slices

blocks.md:
In earlier generations, core nodes spoke specialised telecom protocols. The 5G core is built as a **service-based architecture** (SBA): network functions (NFs) expose HTTP APIs to each other. Tiny example: the **AMF** (Access and Mobility Management Function, not the AKA field of lesson 6), which handles a phone's registration, calls an API on the **AUSF** (Authentication Server Function) to authenticate it, and the AUSF calls the **UDM** for credentials. To find each other, NFs register with and discover through the **NRF** (Network Repository Function).

That makes 5G core security look like web API security. [TS 33.501](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133500_133599/133501/19.07.00_60/ts_133501v190700p.pdf) clause 5.9.2 requires, among others: mutual authentication between NF service consumer and producer when they talk directly; confidentiality, integrity and replay protection for discovery and registration; that the NRF can hide internal topology from other networks; and that each NF "shall validate all incoming messages".

**Authorisation with OAuth 2.0.** The NRF "shall act as authorization server" (clause 5.9.2.2), and clause 13.4.1 says how. An NF wanting a service requests an access token with the OAuth 2.0 **client credentials grant** (the NF asks on its own behalf; no user is involved). Tokens are **JWTs** (JSON Web Tokens) protected with JWS (JSON Web Signature); the spec does not recommend the MAC option because of pre-shared key management, so in practice the NRF signs and producers verify with its public key. The token's scope lists the services allowed per NF type, optionally narrowed further. Support is mandatory for NRF and NFs.

**The edge: SEPP.** The **SEPP** (Security Edge Protection Proxy) sits at the edge of a 5G operator network (a **PLMN**, public land mobile network, named by its MCC and MNC) and protects all control-plane messages to other networks over the **N32** interface. N32-c is the control connection where two SEPPs authenticate each other and agree security; N32-f carries the forwarded messages. Between two SEPPs with no intermediary, N32-f uses TLS. When IPX providers sit in between, operators use either TLS or the **PRINS** protocol (PRotocol for N32 INterconnect Security): with PRINS the SEPPs encrypt chosen message elements with JSON Web Encryption (JWE), and IPX providers that must modify messages sign their changes with JWS, so the receiving SEPP can see who changed what.

scenes.caption: Before any traffic, the two SEPPs set up N32-c: they authenticate each other with certificates and negotiate cipher suites and protection policy.
A roaming phone registers. The visited AMF's request crosses N32-f. With PRINS, the SEPP encrypts sensitive elements (JWE) and IPX providers may only add signed patches (JWS).
The home SEPP checks that the network ID claimed in the 3gpp-Sbi-Originating-Network-Id header belongs to the peer's certificate, then forwards to the AUSF.
Inside the home network, the AUSF needs an NRF-signed token whose scope allows the UDM service it calls. The UDM's SIDF turns the SUCI back into the SUPI.
A peer that claims to speak for a network not in its certificate is discarded at the home SEPP: the 5G version of the category 2 check, bound to an authenticated peer.

blocks.code:
# Toy 5G core checks: SEPP origin check (TS 33.501 5.9.3.2) and NRF token scope (13.4.1)
import json
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.ed25519 import Ed25519PrivateKey
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature

PEER_CERT_PLMNS = {"208-01"}          # PLMN IDs in the peer SEPP's certificate

def sepp_receive(msg):
    claimed = msg["headers"]["3gpp-Sbi-Originating-Network-Id"]
    if claimed not in PEER_CERT_PLMNS:
        return f"discard: peer SEPP may not speak for {claimed}"
    return "forward to NF"

nrf_key = Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()            # NRF = OAuth 2.0 server
def nrf_issue(claims):
    body = json.dumps(claims, sort_keys=True).encode()
    return body, nrf_key.sign(body)

def producer_accepts(token, wanted_scope):        # e.g. the UDM checking a request
    body, sig = token
    try:
        nrf_key.public_key().verify(sig, body)
    except InvalidSignature:
        return "401: token not signed by our NRF"
    return "200 OK" if wanted_scope in json.loads(body)["scope"].split() else "403: scope"

print(sepp_receive({"headers": {"3gpp-Sbi-Originating-Network-Id": "208-01"}}))
print(sepp_receive({"headers": {"3gpp-Sbi-Originating-Network-Id": "234-15"}}))
tok = nrf_issue({"sub": "amf-7", "aud": "UDM", "scope": "nudm-sdm"})
print(producer_accepts(tok, "nudm-sdm"))
print(producer_accepts(tok, "nudm-uecm"))
forged = (tok[0].replace(b"nudm-sdm", b"nudm-sdm nudm-uecm"), tok[1])
print(producer_accepts(forged, "nudm-uecm"))
blocks.caption: Needs the cryptography package (same venv as lesson 8). Real tokens are JWTs per RFC 7519 with fields such as iss, aud, exp; this toy keeps only what the check needs.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
forward to NF
discard: peer SEPP may not speak for 234-15
200 OK
403: scope
401: token not signed by our NRF
```

The SEPP also must perform topology hiding, rate-limit signalling (including SEPP to SEPP), discard malformed messages and apply "anti-spoofing mechanisms that enable cross-layer validation" of addresses and identifiers (clause 5.9.3.2). Each of these answers a lesson 2 to 5 failure.

**Network slicing.** A **slice** is a logical network with its own properties, identified by an **S-NSSAI** (single network slice selection assistance information). Clause 16: a phone gets an allowed slice only after primary authentication, and some slices add **NSSAA** (network slice-specific authentication and authorisation) against an AAA (authentication, authorisation and accounting) server that "may be owned by an external 3rd party enterprise", with credentials separate from the SIM. Slices share infrastructure, so their isolation is only as good as the configuration and the NFs serving them.

**Exposure.** The **NEF** (Network Exposure Function) lets outside applications use network capabilities; the spec forbids it from sending the SUPI or internal identifiers outside the operator.

SEPP and OAuth protect only what passes through them. ENISA warned in 2018 that 5G risked "repeating history", and as long as networks still interwork with SS7 and Diameter for older phones and roaming partners, the old interfaces stay attack surfaces.

blocks.question: A message arrives at your home SEPP over N32 from a peer whose certificate lists PLMN (public land mobile network, an operator network ID) 208-01, but its 3gpp-Sbi-Originating-Network-Id header says 234-15 (your own network). What should the SEPP do?
options: Forward it, because it claims to come from your own network
Discard it: the claimed network is not one the sending SEPP's certificate represents
Forward it, but log a warning
Ask the phone to confirm
blocks.explain: TS 33.501 5.9.3.2: the receiving SEPP checks that the asserted network ID belongs to the sending SEPP (its certificate, N32-f context or configured list) and discards the message if not. Claiming to be your own network is a classic spoof.

blocks.question: An AMF presents a valid NRF-signed token with scope nudm-sdm, and calls a UDM operation that needs nudm-uecm. What should the UDM return?
options: 403: the token is genuine but does not grant this service
200 OK: any signed token is enough
401: the signature is invalid
It should ask the NRF to widen the scope automatically
blocks.explain: Authentication (valid signature) and authorisation (the scope covers this service) are separate checks; TS 33.501 13.4.1 puts the allowed services in the scope claim.

lessons.title: SIM and eSIM: the key in your pocket, and how it gets there

blocks.md:
The SIM is a tiny computer, not a memory chip. Its physical form is a **UICC** (universal integrated circuit card), a smart card that runs the USIM application. The USIM holds the key K shared with the home AuC and runs the AKA functions inside the card (TS 33.102), so K never needs to leave it. In 5G, the operator can even have the USIM compute the SUCI (TS 33.501 6.12.2).

Two more features matter for security:

- **SIM Toolkit** (STK): lets applications on the card send commands to the phone, such as display text, send an SMS or report location.
- **Over-the-air (OTA) updates**: operators manage cards remotely, typically with specially formatted binary SMS that the phone passes straight to the card.

Both are powerful, and both are reachable by anyone who can get a text message to the phone, unless the network and the card filter them.

**Case: Simjacker (2019).** The mobile security firm AdaptiveMobile Security reported an attack it called Simjacker, summarised by [CERT-EU](https://cert.europa.eu/publications/security-advisories/2019-020/pdf) (the EU institutions' computer emergency response team). An SMS carrying SIM Toolkit instructions was crafted to be handed to the card, where an old card application, the **S@T Browser**, executed them. The main attack asked the phone for its location and IMEI (international mobile equipment identity, the handset's serial identity) and sent them out in another SMS, with no sign to the user. CERT-EU reported that it was being actively exploited and that up to 1 billion devices could be affected; devices from nearly every manufacturer were targeted, because the flaw lived on the card.

CERT-EU's recommendation: users can do nothing; operators should "analyse and block suspicious messages that contain S@T Browser commands", and could change card security settings remotely or stop using S@T Browser. The 2026 ITU report generalises this: block binary OTA SMS except from allow-listed sources.

blocks.title: Simjacker: the card as the attacker's agent

scenes.caption: A binary SMS containing SIM Toolkit instructions is sent to the target. Any phone, modem or bulk SMS account can send SMS.
The handset passes the message to the card without showing anything. The S@T Browser on the card executes the instructions.
The card uses STK commands to ask the handset for its location and IMEI, then has it send them in a new SMS.
Defence: the operator filters binary SMS carrying S@T commands, or anything OTA not from its own platform, before it reaches the phone.

blocks.md:
**eSIM.** An **eUICC** (embedded UICC) is a SIM soldered into the device that can hold several operator **profiles**, downloaded remotely. The GSMA's consumer **RSP** (remote SIM provisioning) specification, [SGP.22](https://www.gsma.com/esim/wp-content/uploads/2023/12/SGP.22-v3.1.pdf), defines the parties: the operator's **SM-DP+** (subscription manager data preparation, enhanced) server prepares and serves profiles, and the **LPA** (local profile assistant) on the device fetches them. Each eUICC has an **EID** (eUICC identifier).

To start a download the user usually gets an **Activation Code**, often as a QR code: a format digit, the SM-DP+ address and a **Matching ID**, joined by `$`. SGP.22's example is `1$SMDP.EXAMPLE.COM$04386-AGYFT-A74Y8-3F815`. An optional flag says a **Confirmation Code** is also required, which the operator gives the user "separately from the Activation Code". The SM-DP+ "SHALL limit the number of download attempts and the number of Confirmation Code attempts". If the operator knows the EID when the order is placed, the profile is linked to that device.

blocks.caption: Parses the SGP.22 Activation Code format and applies a small issuing policy. Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
SMDP.EXAMPLE.COM 04386-AGYFT-A74Y8-3F815 cc_required = False
  - no Confirmation Code, no EID binding: any holder can download it
  - code sent to a mailbox an attacker may already control
  - issued right after a number or SIM change: handle as a SIM swap
SMDP.EXAMPLE.COM 04386-AGYFT-A74Y8-3F815 cc_required = True
  - ok
```

An activation code without a Confirmation Code or EID binding is a **bearer secret**: whoever holds it can claim the line. Issuing one is, for account security, the same act as handing over a new SIM card, which is the subject of the next lesson.

The SIM is a computer that holds the subscriber's key and runs code. Protect what can reach it (filter OTA and binary SMS) and treat every way of putting a number onto a new card or eSIM as a credential reset.

blocks.question: Why could Simjacker work on phones from almost every manufacturer?
options: All those phones ran the same operating system version
It exploited a bug in the radio chipset of every phone
It used SS7 to change each phone's firmware
The vulnerable software was the S@T Browser on the SIM card, and phones passed the SMS to the card
blocks.explain: CERT-EU notes the attack depends on software on the UICC, not the device. Handsets forward such messages to the card, so the brand of phone did not matter; that is also why the fix sat with operators and card settings.

blocks.question: An operator emails eSIM activation QR codes with no Confirmation Code and no EID binding. What is the main risk?
options: The QR code will not scan on older phones
The SM-DP+ will run out of profiles
Anyone who obtains the email can download the profile and take over the number
The phone number will change
blocks.explain: Without a Confirmation Code or EID binding, the Activation Code alone identifies the order, so it acts as a bearer secret. Email accounts are a common attacker foothold, so delivery channel and second factor both matter.

lessons.title: SIM swaps and port-outs: an identity problem, not a radio problem

blocks.md:
The prerequisite lesson "Wearing MFA down: SIM swaps, push fatigue and Uber 2022" showed the attack from the account owner's side: a criminal persuades or bribes a carrier to move the victim's number. This lesson looks at the two organisations that can stop it: the **carrier**, which moves numbers, and the **relying party** (a bank, an email provider), which decides whether to trust a number.

The US FCC (Federal Communications Commission) [defines](https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-397990A1.pdf) both forms. **SIM swapping**: a bad actor convinces the victim's wireless provider to transfer the victim's service and number to a device the bad actor holds. **Port-out fraud**: posing as the victim, the bad actor opens an account with a *different* provider and has the number ported (moved) to it. Neither touches radio or signalling: both are failures of **identity verification** at the carrier.

**Case: Jack Dorsey's Twitter account (2019).** On 30 August 2019, offensive tweets were posted from the account of Twitter's chief executive, Jack Dorsey, for about 20 minutes. [Engadget](https://www.engadget.com/2019-08-30-jack-dorsey-twitter-hack-sms.html) noted they were sent through Cloudhopper, the SMS service Twitter had bought in 2010. Twitter's statement: "The phone number associated with the account was compromised due to a security oversight by the mobile provider. This allowed an unauthorized person to compose and send tweets via text message from the phone number."

No password was needed: an old feature trusted the phone number itself as the login. On 4 September Twitter temporarily turned off tweeting by SMS, saying it would bring it back "in markets that depend on SMS for reliable communication" ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/security/twitter-halts-feature-enabled-hack-ceo-s-account-n1049766)).

blocks.title: Dorsey 2019: the number was the credential (not to scale)

scenes.caption: Day 0 (30 August 2019): through what Twitter called a security oversight by the mobile provider, the attacker gains control of the phone number.
Texts from that number are treated as the account owner by Twitter's legacy SMS-to-tweet feature, so tweets go out with no password and no second factor.
Twitter secures the account the same day. Five days later it switches off tweeting by SMS, closing the channel that trusted a phone number alone.

blocks.md: **Carrier controls.** The FCC's Report and Order (FCC 23-95, released 16 November 2023) requires wireless providers to use secure methods of authenticating a customer before a SIM change or port, to keep records of SIM change requests, to have processes for failed authentication attempts, to train employees on SIM swap and port-out fraud, to keep customer-facing staff from customer data until the customer is authenticated, to notify customers immediately of SIM change and port-out requests, and to offer free account **locks**. Compliance waited on paperwork review; Wireline Competition Bureau notices published in the Federal Register on 17 and 18 November 2026 require compliance from 17 December 2026 for the SIM change rules and 18 December 2026 for the port-out rules ([notice](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-11-17/pdf/2026-23400.pdf)).

Other playbooks from the [ITU report](https://www.itu.int/en/ITU-T/extcoop/figisymposium/Documents/ITU_SIT_WG_Technical%20report%20on%20the%20SS7%20vulnerabilities%20and%20their%20impact%20on%20DFS%20transactions_f.pdf): notify the current SIM and wait for a response before a swap, a 2 to 4 hour hold before handing over a new SIM, and challenge questions. CISA's advice to highly targeted people: set a carrier account PIN and MFA on the carrier account ([guidance](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-12/guidance-mobile-communications-best-practices.pdf)).

**Relying-party controls.** [NIST SP 800-63B-4](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html) classes phone-delivered codes as a **restricted** authenticator, says verifiers "SHOULD consider risk indicators (e.g., device swap, SIM change, number porting ...)" before sending one, and requires a phishing-resistant option at AAL2. Operators can expose those signals: the **CAMARA** open-source API project's [SIM Swap API](https://github.com/camaraproject/SimSwap) answers "when did the last SIM swap occur?" and "has one occurred in the last n hours?" (1 to 2400). Its definition counts a new SIM, a port to another provider and a new line on an old number as SIM swaps.

The durable fix is to stop using the number as an authenticator. CISA's mobile guidance: "Do not use SMS as a second factor", enrol FIDO passkeys or security keys, and then disable SMS, because leaving it enrolled creates "a weak, exploitable fallback mechanism".

blocks.caption: Weights and thresholds are illustrative, not from any standard; tune them on your own fraud data. Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
routine login            score   0  proceed
new phone, same SIM      score  15  proceed
SIM changed yesterday    score  40  step up: require the passkey, never SMS
swap then payee + reset  score  75  hold: no SMS, verify with a passkey or an out-of-band call to known details
```

The fourth row is the classic pattern the ITU report suggests banks check for: a SIM swap request close in time to adding a payee or resetting credentials. Note the step-up never falls back to SMS: after a recent SIM change, the SMS channel may belong to the attacker.

blocks.title: Risk score per case, with step-up at 30 and hold at 60

scenes.caption: Scores from the code. A new phone alone (15) is common and stays below the step-up line at 30.
A SIM change within 72 hours crosses 30: require the passkey. Combined with a new device and a payee or password change, the score passes 60: hold the action.

blocks.md: A phone number is an account at someone else's company. Carriers must verify people before moving numbers; everyone else should treat a recent SIM change as a red flag and stop letting SMS alone prove identity.

blocks.question: A bank's fraud check says the customer's number had a SIM swap 6 hours ago, and the customer is now asking to add a new payee. What should the bank do?
options: Send an SMS code to confirm, since SMS is a second factor
Hold or step up with a factor not tied to the number, such as a registered passkey, or call back on independently known details
Approve it, because the password was correct
Ask the customer to reply STOP
blocks.explain: Right after a SIM swap the SMS channel may be controlled by the attacker, so an SMS code proves nothing. NIST lists SIM change as a risk indicator before using the phone channel, and the ITU report recommends exactly this timing check.

blocks.question: In the Dorsey case, which control would most directly have prevented the tweets?
options: Not accepting posts authenticated only by the sending phone number
A longer Twitter password
Encrypting tweets
Disabling 2G on the phone
blocks.explain: The SMS-to-tweet feature trusted the number as the credential, so no password was involved. Twitter's own response was to switch that feature off. Radio-layer settings are irrelevant: the number was moved at the carrier.

lessons.title: Lawful interception: a built-in wiretap, and the Athens affair

blocks.md: Most countries require operators to be able to intercept specific subscribers' communications when presented with a legal order. That capability is built into the network on purpose. From an attacker's view, it is a ready-made surveillance system, plus a list of who the authorities are watching.

[3GPP TS 33.127](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133100_133199/133127/19.08.00_60/ts_133127v190800p.pdf) describes the architecture. A **LEA** (law enforcement agency) presents a **warrant**. Inside the operator, the **ADMF** (LI administration function) contains the **LICF** (control function: "the master record of all sensitive information and LI configuration data", and responsible for auditing other LI components) and the **LIPF** (provisioning function). The LIPF provisions **POIs** (points of interception) inside network functions over the **LI_X1** interface. A POI that detects the target's traffic sends **xIRI** (intercept-related information: who, when, where) over LI_X2 and **xCC** (content of communication) over LI_X3 to the **MDF** (mediation and delivery function), which hands IRI and CC to the agency's **LEMF** (law enforcement monitoring facility) over handover interfaces HI2 and HI3. HI1 carries the warrant administration.

blocks.title: The lawful path, the audit, and a rogue path

scenes.caption: Lawful path: a warrant reaches the ADMF, which provisions a POI. Intercepted IRI and content flow through mediation to the agency.
The LICF holds the master list of warrants and audits POIs. An audit asks each network element what it is actually intercepting.
Athens 2004 to 2005: rogue software inside the switches drove the built-in interception functions directly, never through the management system, so no warrant record existed.
Comparing what the switches intercept with the warrants on record exposes the extra taps: the audit the IEEE Spectrum analysis recommends.

blocks.md: **Case: the Athens affair.** Vassilis Prevelakis and Diomidis Spinellis, university researchers in computer science and software engineering, reconstructed it for [IEEE Spectrum](https://spectrum.ieee.org/the-athens-affair) (2007). Beginning in the run-up to the August 2004 Athens Olympics, about 100 phones on the Vodafone Greece network were tapped, including the prime minister's. Rogue software in Vodafone's Ericsson AXE switches used the switches' own lawful-interception functions. Vodafone had not bought Ericsson's interception management system, so the taps never appeared in any operator interface. According to the Greek privacy authority, the software modified the switch's command parser so that commands followed by six spaces disabled the transaction log and its alarm. Intercepted calls were copied to "shadow" phones, which also received location and call details by automated text.

It surfaced on 24 January 2005: the perpetrators updated their planted software, the update broke the forwarding of some text messages, and the undelivered messages triggered an automated failure report. Ericsson, called in to diagnose it, examined the switches' memory dumps, found the software and alerted Vodafone on 4 March 2005; Vodafone removed it on 7 March, which the authors say almost certainly alerted the perpetrators.

**What the authors say would have caught it.** An audit "could then find a discrepancy between the numbers monitored by the exchange and the warrants active" in the management system. Logging must be stored where rogue software cannot change it, such as a separate monitoring computer. And response must preserve evidence: logs were kept only five days because of storage space, and the early removal cost the chance to trace the shadow phones.

TS 33.120's list of GSM weaknesses (lesson 6) already said LI was an afterthought in 2G. TS 33.127 now makes the LICF responsible for auditing POIs and MDFs; the code below is that audit in miniature.

blocks.caption: Synthetic warrants and tasks. The important design choice is the data source: ask the network elements directly, not the LI management GUI, because Athens showed the GUI can be bypassed. Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
ok msc-1: W-101
HIGH msc-1: W-102 expired 2026-11-01, tap still active
CRITICAL msc-2: tap on +44700900777 to +44700555123 has no warrant
```

Two different failures: a lawful tap that outlived its warrant (a compliance and privacy breach), and a tap with no warrant delivering to an ordinary phone number (the Athens pattern).

Lawful interception systems are high-value targets twice over: they can listen, and their warrant lists reveal investigations. Treat the LI system, its management plane and its logs as the most sensitive systems the operator runs.

blocks.question: In the Athens case, why did Vodafone's operators not see the taps in their tools?
options: The taps were encrypted
The taps were run from a satellite
The rogue software used the switches' interception functions directly, and Vodafone had no interception management system installed to display them
The prime minister's phone was on another network
blocks.explain: IEEE Spectrum reports Vodafone had not bought the interception management system, and the rogue code drove the AXE's built-in functions without it, also suppressing the transaction log.

blocks.question: Which audit design would most reliably find an Athens-style tap?
options: Reviewing the list of warrants in the LI management system
Checking that every warrant has been provisioned
Asking engineers whether they set up any taps
Querying each switch for its active intercepts and comparing them with the warrant master list, using logs the switch software cannot alter
blocks.explain: The rogue taps existed only in the switches, so a review that starts from the management system sees nothing. The authors recommend comparing what the exchange actually monitors with the active warrants, with logging rogue software cannot modify.

lessons.title: Salt Typhoon: espionage inside carrier networks (2024 to 2025)

blocks.md:
**Salt Typhoon** is Microsoft's name for a China-based espionage group; in Microsoft's [naming scheme](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/unified-secops/microsoft-threat-actor-naming), "Typhoon indicates origin or attribution to China". Other firms use other names for overlapping activity.

On 13 November 2024 the FBI and CISA issued a [joint statement](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/news/joint-statement-fbi-and-cisa-peoples-republic-china-prc-targeting-commercial-telecommunications): PRC-affiliated actors had compromised networks at multiple telecommunications companies "to enable the theft of customer call records data, the compromise of private communications of a limited number of individuals who are primarily involved in government or political activity, and the copying of certain information that was subject to U.S. law enforcement requests pursuant to court orders". The last item ties straight to the previous lesson: data from the lawful-interception process was itself a target.
