In December 2024 CISA told highly targeted people to "assume that all communications between mobile devices ... and internet services are at risk of interception", to use end-to-end encrypted messaging, FIDO authentication and no SMS second factor ([guidance](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2024-12/guidance-mobile-communications-best-practices.pdf)).

**How they operated.** The joint advisory [AA25-239A](https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa25-239a) (released August 2025 and revised the next month, from CISA, NSA, FBI and many international partners) compiles what investigations found, from activity since at least 2021:
- *Targets*: large backbone routers of major providers, provider edge (PE) and customer edge (CE) routers, and trusted provider-to-provider or provider-to-customer links used to pivot into other networks.
- *Initial access*: known, patched vulnerabilities, including Ivanti Connect Secure (CVE-2024-21887, chained with CVE-2023-46805), Palo Alto PAN-OS GlobalProtect (CVE-2024-3400) and Cisco IOS XE web UI (CVE-2023-20198 with CVE-2023-20273). CISA's December 2024 guide said no novel activity had been observed: the compromises matched existing weaknesses.
- *Persistence*: adding attacker addresses to access control lists (often named "access-list 20"), opening SSH and web servers on high non-standard ports, adding SSH keys.

- *Collection*: packet captures on routers, especially of **TACACS+** (Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus, the router admin login protocol, TCP port 49); redirecting a router's TACACS+ server to their own address; recovering a shared secret stored with reversible "Type 7" encoding.
- *Hiding and exfiltration*: running tools in the routers' on-box Linux container (Cisco Guest Shell), which device logs barely watch, and moving data out through GRE (generic routing encapsulation) or IPsec (IP security, a protocol suite that authenticates and encrypts IP packets) tunnels.

blocks.title: The intrusion path in AA25-239A, and where defenders cut it

scenes.caption: Entry through an internet-facing device with a known, patched CVE. Patching the listed CVEs closes this step.
On the router: ACL entries for actor addresses, new management ports, packet capture of TACACS+ logins, or the TACACS+ server pointed at the actor.
Tools run inside the router's Linux container, which normal syslog barely sees; data leaves through tunnels built to look like expected traffic.
Trusted interconnections to customers and other providers become the next entry point, which is why one carrier's compromise is everyone's problem.
Defender cuts: patch edge devices; management only from an out-of-band network; config from a central source of truth with drift alerts; AAA accounting; alerts on captures, containers and tunnels.

blocks.md:
**The advisory's defences** (selected): put all management services in a dedicated out-of-band network or management VRF (virtual routing and forwarding instance) and block its egress except to approved collectors; default-deny management ACLs; SNMPv3 (Simple Network Management Protocol version 3) with authentication and privacy only, no default community strings, and alerts on SNMP SET (write) changes to AAA, tunnels, mirroring or ACLs; AAA (authentication, authorisation and accounting) command accounting so container use is recorded; hunt for `guestshell enable` and on-box capture commands; flag TACACS+ traffic to unapproved addresses.

CISA's [December 2024 guide](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/enhanced-visibility-and-hardening-guidance-communications-infrastructure) adds: "Store configurations centrally and push to devices. Do not allow devices to be the trusted source of truth for their configuration." That makes drift detection possible.

blocks.code:
# Diff a router's running config against the golden copy and rank changes using
# the signals in CISA advisory AA25-239A. Synthetic config; documentation IP ranges.
import re
golden = """hostname pe-7
tacacs server MGMT address ipv4 10.0.0.5
snmp-server group OPS v3 priv
access-list 20 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255""".splitlines()
running = """hostname pe-7
tacacs server MGMT address ipv4 203.0.113.9
snmp-server group OPS v3 priv
snmp-server community public RW
access-list 20 permit 10.0.0.0 0.0.0.255
access-list 20 permit 198.51.100.44
ip http server
interface Tunnel7
 tunnel destination 198.51.100.44
iox""".splitlines()

RULES = [  # (pattern, why it matters)
    (r"^tacacs server .* address ipv4 (?!10\.)", "AAA server moved off the management net"),
    (r"^snmp-server community (public|private)", "default SNMP community string"),
    (r"^access-list \d+ permit (?!10\.)", "ACL now permits an outside address"),
    (r"^ip http server", "web UI enabled (CVE-2023-20198 entry point)"),
    (r"^interface Tunnel", "new tunnel interface (GRE used for exfiltration)"),
    (r"^iox", "app hosting on: Guest Shell containers possible"),
]
for line in running:
    if line in golden:
        continue
    hits = [why for pat, why in RULES if re.search(pat, line.strip())]
    tag = "ALERT " if hits else "review"
    print(f"{tag} {line.strip():45} {'; '.join(hits)}".rstrip())
blocks.caption: Configuration lines are simplified IOS-style syntax on synthetic data with documentation IP ranges; adapt patterns to your platforms. Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
ALERT  tacacs server MGMT address ipv4 203.0.113.9   AAA server moved off the management net
ALERT  snmp-server community public RW               default SNMP community string
ALERT  access-list 20 permit 198.51.100.44           ACL now permits an outside address
ALERT  ip http server                                web UI enabled (CVE-2023-20198 entry point)
ALERT  interface Tunnel7                             new tunnel interface (GRE used for exfiltration)
review tunnel destination 198.51.100.44
ALERT  iox                                           app hosting on: Guest Shell containers possible
```

A diff against a central golden copy turns the advisory's indicators into alerts. Note the tunnel destination equals the address just added to the ACL: correlating two weak signals makes a strong one.

Salt Typhoon worked through routers and management planes, not through exotic telecom protocols. Patch edge devices, keep management out of band, make a central copy the source of truth for configuration, and treat lawful-interception data as a prime target.

blocks.question: Why does AA25-239A warn not to rely on device syslog alone on routers that support Guest Shell?
options: Syslog is always disabled on routers
Guest Shell encrypts syslog
Syslog cannot record IP addresses
Activity inside the on-box container is not closely monitored, so you need AAA command accounting, container logs and off-box flow data too
blocks.explain: The advisory says activities and data in the container are not monitored closely and recommends combining syslog, AAA command accounting, container logs and off-box telemetry.

blocks.question: A router's running config shows the TACACS+ server changed to an address outside your management network. What is the most important concern?
options: The router will boot slower
Administrator logins may now be sent to an attacker, who can capture credentials
SNMP will stop working
The router's clock will drift
blocks.explain: AA25-239A reports actors redirecting TACACS+ to their own infrastructure to capture authentication attempts. Treat it as a credential compromise: revert from the golden config, rotate the TACACS+ secret and admin credentials, and hunt for other changes.

lessons.title: Satellite links: segments, footprints and cleartext GEO traffic

blocks.md:
A satellite network has three parts, usually called segments:

- **Space segment**: the satellites. A communications satellite carries **transponders**, on-board units that receive a signal from the ground and send it back down on another frequency.
- **Ground segment**: hubs and gateways that connect satellite links to the internet or a private network, plus the network operations centres and management systems that run the service.
- **User segment**: dishes and modems (terminals) at homes, ships, aircraft, mines, phone masts.

**GEO** (geostationary) satellites orbit so that they appear fixed in the sky. The "Don't Look Up" paper (Zhang et al., ACM CCS 2025) explains the consequence: each transponder's **footprint** can cover up to a third of Earth's surface, and the forward link from hub to terminals is broadcast across that whole area. Anyone in the footprint with a dish can receive it. Satellite TV has encrypted its content for decades for that reason; the question is whether IP traffic does too.

**The 2025 study.** Wenyi Morty Zhang, Annie Dai, Keegan Ryan, Dave Levin, Nadia Heninger and Aaron Schulman (UC San Diego and the University of Maryland) published "Don't Look Up: There Are Sensitive Internal Links in the Clear on GEO Satellites" at ACM CCS 2025. From their abstract: they performed "the first broad scan of IP traffic on 39 GEO satellites across 25 distinct longitudes with 411 transponders using consumer-grade equipment", and found "50% of GEO links contained cleartext IP traffic". They observed unencrypted cellular backhaul including call and text contents, industrial control traffic for utilities, military asset tracking, retail inventory and in-flight Wi-Fi. They note a receiving station costs about USD 600.

The most striking finding for this course: **T-Mobile cellular backhaul** (the link from remote masts to the core) carried plaintext SMS and voice, user internet traffic and signalling; its IMS (IP Multimedia Subsystem, the 4G voice and SMS service) traffic used IPsec with a null cipher. In a 9-hour recording they saw 2,711 users' phone numbers. The radio link from phone to mast was encrypted; the backhaul behind it was not, which echoes TS 33.120's old complaint about GSM encryption stopping at the base station.

blocks.title: How often encryption was on, by layer (Don't Look Up, 2025)

scenes.caption: Satellite TV transponders that use MPEG framing (the Moving Picture Experts Group video transport format) mostly scramble content: two thirds did.
Non-TV links using MPEG framing scrambled only 10% of the time; links using GSE (Generic Stream Encapsulation) had encryption on only 20% of the time.
At the network layer, only 6% of the transponders where IP was recovered consistently carried IPsec. Overall, half of GEO links had cleartext IP traffic.

blocks.md:
**Why it stays unencrypted**, from the paper's discussion: encryption that was disabled by misconfiguration or a software update "failed open", with no sign to operators; terminals may need extra licence fees to use their crypto subsystem; Panasonic Avionics told the authors encryption could cost 20 to 30% of capacity; IPsec adds 20 to 30 bytes per packet, much for small voice packets; some users choose unencrypted links for reliability; providers said encryption made troubleshooting impossible; and products still show artefacts of old US export controls, such as optional 56-bit keys. The paper quotes a 2022 NSA advisory on GEO links: "Most of these links are unencrypted, relying on frequency separation or predictable frequency hopping rather than encryption".

**Disclosure and fix.** The team disclosed to T-Mobile on 19 December 2024, and "T-Mobile quickly enabled encryption"; disclosures to the US military, Walmart Mexico, AT&T, Intelsat, Panasonic Avionics and others followed.

**Defender view.**

- *Prevent*: treat every satellite hop as an untrusted network. Encrypt at the network layer (IPsec or another VPN) or the application layer (TLS), in addition to any link-layer option, so that one failing-open layer does not expose traffic.
- *Detect*: verify, do not assume. The authors found that "no auditing tools exist that allow vendors to audit the security of their own satellite backhaul", and found organisations that had intended to enable encryption but had not. Capture your own link's traffic at your own terminal and check it.
- *Respond*: if cleartext is found, rotate any credentials or keys that crossed the link, because anyone in the footprint may have recorded them.

blocks.code:
# Audit your OWN satellite link captures: is each flow's payload encrypted?
# Shannon entropy in bits per byte: text sits near 4-5, ciphertext near 8.
import math, hashlib
from collections import Counter

def entropy(data: bytes) -> float:
    n = len(data)
    return -sum(c / n * math.log2(c / n) for c in Counter(data).values())

def pseudo_cipher(n):        # deterministic stand-in for encrypted bytes
    out, i = b"", 0
    while len(out) < n:
        out += hashlib.sha256(i.to_bytes(4, "big")).digest(); i += 1
    return out[:n]

sip = (b"MESSAGE sip:+15550100@ims.example SIP/2.0\r\nVia: SIP/2.0/UDP "
       b"10.1.2.3:5060\r\nContent-Type: application/vnd.3gpp.sms\r\n") * 20
scada = b"\x01\x03\x00\x10\x00\x02\xc5\xce" * 200    # repetitive polling frames
flows = {"cell backhaul (SIP)": sip, "utility polling": scada,
         "ipsec tunnel": pseudo_cipher(2048)}
for name, payload in flows.items():
    h = entropy(payload)
    print(f"{name:20} {h:4.2f} bits/byte  {'looks encrypted' if h > 7.5 else 'CLEARTEXT?'}")
blocks.caption: Audits payloads captured from your own link. Entropy is a hint, not proof: compressed data also looks random, so confirm with protocol headers (an IPsec ESP header or a TLS handshake). Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
cell backhaul (SIP)  5.09 bits/byte  CLEARTEXT?
utility polling      2.75 bits/byte  CLEARTEXT?
ipsec tunnel         7.91 bits/byte  looks encrypted
```

Shannon entropy measures how unpredictable each byte is, on a scale of 0 to 8 bits per byte. Text and repetitive control protocols sit well below 8; good ciphertext is indistinguishable from random and sits just under 8.

Link-layer encryption that silently turns off is worse than none you knew about. Put the protection you rely on at a layer you control and can monitor, such as IPsec or TLS between your own endpoints.

blocks.question: Why can one receiving station observe traffic meant for terminals hundreds of kilometres away?
options: A GEO transponder's forward link is broadcast across a footprint that can cover a third of Earth, so any dish inside it can receive the signal
Satellites forward every packet to every country on purpose
The researchers hacked the satellites
Terminals send copies of their traffic to anyone who asks
blocks.explain: The study was passive: it received broadcasts. GEO footprints are huge by design, which is why confidentiality has to come from encryption, not from location.

blocks.question: The phone-to-mast radio link of a remote mast is encrypted, but its satellite backhaul is not. What can a listener in the footprint see?
options: Nothing: radio encryption protects the whole path
Only encrypted data
Whatever crosses the backhaul in clear: in the T-Mobile case, SMS and call contents, phone numbers and signalling
Only the satellite's position
blocks.explain: Radio encryption ends at the mast. Behind it, the backhaul needs its own protection; the paper found IMS traffic using IPsec with a null cipher, which provides no confidentiality.

lessons.title: Case: the Viasat KA-SAT attack (24 February 2022)

blocks.md:
On the morning Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began, tens of thousands of satellite broadband modems across Europe went offline over the next two hours and did not come back. Nobody touched the satellite. The attackers came in through the **ground segment**, the management network, and used it to send ordinary management commands that disabled the modems.

The service was a consumer broadband partition of the **KA-SAT** network, sold under the Tooway brand. Viasat had bought the business from Eutelsat in 2021, and a Eutelsat subsidiary, Skylogic, still ran the ground operations for Viasat under a transition agreement ([Viasat's incident overview](https://news.viasat.com/blog/corporate/ka-sat-network-cyber-attack-overview)).

blocks.title: 24 February 2022, minutes after 03:00 UTC (from Viasat's report)

scenes.caption: About 03:02 UTC: high volumes of malicious traffic come from SurfBeam2 modems (Viasat consumer modems) in Ukraine, a denial of service that makes it hard for other modems to stay online.
Staff force malicious modems offline, but others appear and continue for several hours. Meanwhile the number of modems online in the partition declines gradually.
From about 04:15 UTC, large numbers of modems across much of Europe leave the network over about 45 minutes, and are not seen trying to rejoin.
The UK government later said the attack began about an hour before the invasion. The primary target is believed to have been the Ukrainian military; others were hit too.

blocks.md:
**What broke**, in Viasat's words: "a ground-based network intrusion by an attacker exploiting a misconfiguration in a VPN appliance to gain remote access to the trusted management segment of the KA-SAT network. The attacker moved laterally through this trusted management network to a specific network segment used to manage and operate the network, and then used this network access to execute legitimate, targeted management commands on a large number of residential modems simultaneously." The commands "overwrote key data in flash memory on the modems, rendering the modems unable to access the network, but not permanently unusable".

Viasat found no damage to electrical components, no tampering with modem firmware images and no supply-chain interference; the modems could be restored by a factory reset. It said there was no evidence that the satellite or its ground infrastructure "were directly involved, impaired or compromised", and no evidence that end-user data was accessed. Some modems were fixed by over-the-air updates; Viasat shipped nearly 30,000 replacements to speed recovery.

**Impact and attribution.** Viasat counted several thousand affected customers in Ukraine and tens of thousands across Europe. On 10 May 2022 the UK, the EU, the US and allies [attributed](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/russia-behind-cyber-attack-with-europe-wide-impact-an-hour-before-ukraine-invasion) the attack to Russia; the UK's NCSC (National Cyber Security Centre) assessed it was "almost certain". The UK statement noted that wind farms in central Europe were also affected, and quoted Viasat: "tens of thousands of terminals have been damaged, made inoperable and cannot be repaired" (an earlier statement than the overview's later finding that modems could be restored by factory reset).

**What stopped it spreading.** The attack stayed in one consumer partition; Viasat's mobility and government users on the same satellite, and its other networks, were not affected. Partitioning limited the blast radius.

**Defender lessons** (our reading; Viasat did not publish its mitigations):

- *The entry was an edge device*: a misconfigured VPN appliance. Inventory and harden remote-access appliances; they were also Salt Typhoon's door (lesson 13).
- *The management plane was "trusted"*: once inside, the attacker could reach the segment that commands every modem. Require strong authentication and separate zones *inside* management networks, not only at their edge.
- *Legitimate commands were the delivery path*: the attacker used the management system's own command channel. SentinelLabs, the research team of the security firm SentinelOne, later described a modem wiper it named AcidRain, and Viasat told journalists the analysis matched its findings: a destructive program run on the modems through a legitimate management command. So fleet-wide operations need their own guardrails: who may issue them, from where, to how many devices at once, with whose approval.
- *Recovery is a capacity plan*: spares, factory-reset procedures and over-the-air repair paths decided before the incident.

blocks.caption: An illustrative guardrail for any device-fleet manager (modems, routers, phones, meters), not Viasat's design. Thresholds are examples. Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
config_push   x 1,200: run in waves of 50, watch health
firmware_push x 8,000: run in waves of 50, watch health
flash_write   x40,000: BLOCK: issued from 172.16.9.4, not an ops jump host; 40,000 devices needs two approvers; no change ticket
```

Even approved jobs run in waves: if the first 50 devices go dark, the job stops before 40,000 do. A rule like this does not stop an attacker who controls the approvers' accounts too, which is why it sits on top of, not instead of, strong authentication.

KA-SAT was hit through its ground segment: a VPN appliance, a trusted management network and legitimate commands sent at scale. Protect the management plane like the product itself, and limit how much any single command can break.

blocks.question: Which statement best matches Viasat's account of how the modems were disabled?
options: Legitimate management commands, sent from inside the management network after a VPN misconfiguration was exploited, overwrote data in the modems' flash memory
Malicious firmware was pushed through the normal update server
The satellite was hacked from space
Users downloaded malware onto their PCs
blocks.explain: Viasat found no evidence its firmware distribution or update processes were used, and no evidence the satellite or ground infrastructure itself was compromised. The destructive step travelled over normal management functionality, reached through a misconfigured VPN appliance; it ran a wiper on the modems rather than replacing their firmware.

blocks.question: Which design property limited the damage to one part of the KA-SAT service?
options: The satellite's solar panels
Partitioning: the attack was confined to a single consumer-oriented partition, so mobility and government users were unaffected
All modems used different passwords
The modems were made by many vendors
blocks.explain: Viasat says the incident was localised to a single consumer partition and did not affect directly managed mobility or government users or other networks. Segmentation bounded the blast radius.

lessons.title: GNSS: how a receiver finds position and time, and what jamming does

blocks.md:
**GNSS** (Global Navigation Satellite System) is the general name for satellite navigation: the US GPS (Global Positioning System), Europe's Galileo and others. Each satellite broadcasts its precise time and its orbit. A receiver notes when each signal arrives; the delay times the speed of light gives a distance. With exact clocks, three distances would fix a point in space.

But a receiver's clock is cheap and wrong by an unknown offset b, so each measured distance is off by c times b. That distance-plus-clock-error is called a **pseudorange**. Four unknowns (x, y, z and b) need at least four satellites. The output is position, navigation and **timing** (PNT): solving for b gives very accurate time, and a lot of infrastructure uses GNSS only for that.

blocks.caption: Pseudorange to satellite i: the true distance from receiver position r to satellite position s_i, plus the speed of light c times the receiver clock bias b.

blocks.code:
# Solve position (x, y, z) and clock bias b from 4+ pseudoranges (synthetic, km)
C = 299792.458   # km/s
SATS = [(15600, 7540, 20140), (18760, 2750, 18610),
        (17610, 14630, 13480), (19170, 610, 18390), (-1000, 16000, 21000)]
TRUE = (-41.8, -16.8, 6370.0)   # receiver on the surface

def dist(a, b): return sum((p - q) ** 2 for p, q in zip(a, b)) ** 0.5

def solve(A, v):   # Gaussian elimination
    n = len(v); M = [r[:] + [x] for r, x in zip(A, v)]
    for i in range(n):
        p = max(range(i, n), key=lambda r: abs(M[r][i])); M[i], M[p] = M[p], M[i]
        for r in range(n):
            if r != i:
                f = M[r][i] / M[i][i]; M[r] = [a - f * b for a, b in zip(M[r], M[i])]
    return [M[i][n] / M[i][i] for i in range(n)]

def fix(pr):   # Gauss-Newton least squares
    x = [0.0, 0.0, 6370.0, 0.0]   # x[3] = c * bias, in km
    for _ in range(8):
        J, r = [], []
        for s, p in zip(SATS, pr):
            d = dist(x[:3], s)
            J.append([(x[k] - s[k]) / d for k in range(3)] + [1.0])
            r.append(p - (d + x[3]))
        JtJ = [[sum(a[i] * a[j] for a in J) for j in range(4)] for i in range(4)]
        Jtr = [sum(a[i] * e for a, e in zip(J, r)) for i in range(4)]
        x = [a + b for a, b in zip(x, solve(JtJ, Jtr))]
    return x

bias_ms = 0.5
honest = [dist(TRUE, s) + C * bias_ms / 1000 for s in SATS]
for name, pr in [("honest", honest), ("all delayed 3 ms", [p + C * 0.003 for p in honest])]:
    x = fix(pr)
    print(f"{name:17} error {dist(x[:3], TRUE)*1000:8.3f} m   clock {x[3] / C * 1000:6.3f} ms")
blocks.caption: Synthetic satellite positions (about 26,500 km from Earth's centre, like GPS orbits) and a receiver on the surface. Gauss-Newton least squares; no libraries needed. Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
honest            error    0.000 m   clock  0.500 ms
all delayed 3 ms  error    0.000 m   clock  3.500 ms
```

The second line is the key insight for timing users. Delay every signal by the same 3 ms and the solver puts all of it into the clock term: the position is still perfect, but the time is 3 ms wrong. A receiver used only for time, on a phone mast or in a substation, has no position change to notice.

**Why telecom cares.** A 2026 preprint on spoofing in mobile networks ([abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11398)) notes that TDD (time division duplex) mobile networks need synchronisation within plus or minus 1.5 microseconds (3GPP TS 38.104), with GNSS-disciplined clocks the predominant timing source, so spoofed time can corrupt timing "across all downstream base stations". CISA lists communications network operations among the critical infrastructure uses of GPS ([CISA Insights](https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/2023-02/CISA-Insights_GPS-Interference_508.pdf)).

blocks.title: Four ranges, one clock, and two kinds of interference

scenes.caption: Each satellite's signal gives one pseudorange. Four of them fix the receiver's three coordinates and its clock error.
Jamming: a transmitter floods the band with noise. The very weak satellite signals are drowned out, and the receiver loses its fix: loud and obvious.
Spoofing: counterfeit signals, stronger than the real ones, make the receiver compute a wrong but self-consistent position or time, with nothing obviously failing.

blocks.md: **Jamming versus spoofing**, as the EU Aviation Safety Agency defines them in Safety Information Bulletin [2022-02R4](https://ad.easa.europa.eu/blob/EASA_SIB_2022_02R4.pdf/SIB_2022-02R4_1) (3 July 2026): jamming is intentional radio interference that "prevents receivers from locking onto satellites signals"; spoofing broadcasts counterfeit signals "causing them to compute incorrect position, navigation, and timing (PNT) data". EASA reports that jamming and spoofing have increased since February 2022, especially around conflict zones such as the eastern Mediterranean, Black Sea, Middle East, Baltic Sea and Arctic. Jamming is usually immediately noticeable; spoofing "may be more difficult and not immediate" to detect, "thus posing more safety risk".

Observed effects include spurious terrain "PULL UP" alerts that led to steep climbs, corrupted ADS-B (Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast, the position reports aircraft broadcast), wrong position even after leaving the affected area, and wrong time in clocks and flight management systems. EASA recommends keeping non-GNSS navigation aids (instrument landing systems, distance measuring equipment and very high frequency (VHF) omnidirectional range beacons) operational and having crews cross-check position by non-GNSS means.

**Case: Denver, January 2022.** CISA describes a 33-hour GPS interference event near Denver International Airport. Pilots noticed first; the FAA (Federal Aviation Administration) issued a notice to aircraft. Rail and road systems and communications towers using GPS timing were also affected. The cause was an emitter transmitting unintentionally in the GPS L1 band; affected receivers on the ground were within about 50 nautical miles, and aircraft up to about 230 nautical miles away at altitude. The FCC's Enforcement Bureau found and shut it down. Systems with "resilient alternate timing" saw minor or no degradation.

CISA's detection tip is simple: the constellation is very reliable, so "multiple receivers should not lose reception at the same time"; if several receivers of different makes lose GPS together, suspect interference and report it.

A GNSS receiver solves for position and its own clock from at least four pseudoranges. Jamming removes the signals and is loud; spoofing replaces them and can be quiet, and a uniform delay shifts time without moving the position.

blocks.question: A spoofer delays every satellite signal reaching a static timing receiver by the same amount. What does the receiver report?
options: A position far from its real location
No fix at all
A warning that it is being spoofed
The correct position but a wrong time
blocks.explain: In the pseudorange equation a common delay is absorbed entirely by the clock term c times b, as the code shows: zero position error, clock off by the delay. A timing-only receiver has no position jump to notice.

blocks.question: According to EASA, why is spoofing considered a bigger safety risk to aircraft than jamming?
options: Spoofing equipment is always more powerful
Spoofing only affects military aircraft
Jamming effects are usually immediate and noticeable, while spoofing may be harder to detect and not immediate
Jamming is legal
blocks.explain: EASA SIB 2022-02R4: jamming typically produces immediate, recognisable failures; detection of spoofing may be more difficult and not immediate, thus posing more safety risk.

lessons.title: Detecting GNSS spoofing, and authenticated navigation signals

blocks.md:
A spoofed receiver is not broken: it is calmly computing the answer the spoofer designed. So detection means asking whether that answer is **consistent** with everything else you know: physics, your own clock, other receivers, other sources.

The US Department of Homeland Security's [Resilient PNT Conformance Framework](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/publications/2020_12_resilient_pnt_conformance_framework.pdf) (2020) sets the mindset. Manipulation "can also result in biased or ramping errors within the expected performance bounds that are erroneous and misleading", so a careful attacker stays inside your thresholds. Detection "is generally probabilistic", trading false positives against missed attacks. It defines resilience levels: Level 1 must verify stored data against standards and support full recovery; Level 2 must also identify compromised PNT sources and keep them out of the solution; higher levels bound how far the output may degrade.

**Checks a receiver or its operator can run:**

- *Plausibility*: could the platform really have moved this way? EASA asks crews to cross-check GNSS position against non-GNSS means.
- *Clock self-consistency*: a receiver reports both its clock bias and its clock drift (rate). Normally the bias changes by the drift times elapsed time. A 2026 paper in the journal *Sensors* ([Chen et al.](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12845604/)) uses "the cumulative difference between the estimated clock bias and the bias obtained by integrating clock drift" as its detection statistic, with a fastest alarm delay of 2 seconds or less in their tests.
- *Independent references*: a local oscillator in holdover, a network time source, or other receivers. The telecom preprint from the last lesson correlates anomalies across base stations that share the same GNSS-disciplined master clock.
- *Many receivers at once*: CISA's rule that several receivers should not fail together.

blocks.code:
# Consistency checks on a GNSS receiver's own output (synthetic, 1 record per second)
MAX_MPS = 70          # a truck: faster than this is implausible
MAX_GAP_NS = 100      # allowed gap between clock bias and integrated drift

# t (s), east (m), north (m), clock bias (ns), clock drift (ns/s) as the receiver reports
log = [(0, 0, 0, 100, 1), (1, 20, 0, 101, 1), (2, 40, 0, 102, 1), (3, 60, 0, 103, 1),
       (4, 80, 1, 133, 1), (5, 100, 2, 163, 1), (6, 120, 4, 193, 1), (7, 140, 7, 223, 1),
       (8, 160, 11, 253, 1), (9, 180, 16, 283, 1)]

predicted = log[0][3]           # bias predicted by integrating the drift
prev = log[0]
for t, e, n, bias, drift in log[1:]:
    dt = t - prev[0]
    predicted += drift * dt
    speed = ((e - prev[1])**2 + (n - prev[2])**2) ** 0.5 / dt
    gap = bias - predicted
    alarms = []
    if speed > MAX_MPS:
        alarms.append(f"speed {speed:.0f} m/s")
    if abs(gap) > MAX_GAP_NS:
        alarms.append(f"bias {gap:+.0f} ns away from its own drift")
    print(f"t={t} speed {speed:4.1f} m/s gap {gap:+4.0f} ns",
          "SUSPECT: " + ", ".join(alarms) if alarms else "ok")
    prev = (t, e, n, bias)
blocks.caption: Synthetic log of a vehicle receiver; a spoofer starts pulling time just after t = 3, about 29 ns per second beyond the reported drift, while keeping position smooth. Thresholds are illustrative. Run with python3.

blocks.md:
Output:

```
t=1 speed 20.0 m/s gap   +0 ns ok
t=2 speed 20.0 m/s gap   +0 ns ok
t=3 speed 20.0 m/s gap   +0 ns ok
t=4 speed 20.0 m/s gap  +29 ns ok
t=5 speed 20.0 m/s gap  +58 ns ok
t=6 speed 20.1 m/s gap  +87 ns ok
t=7 speed 20.2 m/s gap +116 ns SUSPECT: bias +116 ns away from its own drift
t=8 speed 20.4 m/s gap +145 ns SUSPECT: bias +145 ns away from its own drift
t=9 speed 20.6 m/s gap +174 ns SUSPECT: bias +174 ns away from its own drift
```

The speed check never fires: the position drifts by a few metres, well inside the 70 m/s limit, exactly DHS's "ramping errors within the expected performance bounds". The clock check accumulates the small per-second inconsistency until it crosses 100 ns at t = 7.

blocks.title: Gap between clock bias and integrated drift during a time pull

scenes.caption: The code's case: the spoofer starts at t = 3 and pulls 29 ns per second. The gap crosses 100 ns between t = 6 and t = 7, so the alarm fires at t = 7.
A patient spoofer pulling only 10 ns per second takes 10 seconds to cross the same threshold: slower attacks are detected later.
Lowering the threshold to 50 ns catches the slow pull sooner, at the cost of more false alarms from ordinary clock noise: the trade-off DHS describes.

blocks.md: **Authenticated navigation data: Galileo OSNMA.** Detection only helps if signals can be faked. Europe's Galileo now signs part of what it broadcasts. **OSNMA** (Open Service Navigation Message Authentication) adds a "digital signature" to Galileo's open-service navigation data, specifically the ephemeris (the satellite's broadcast orbit parameters) and timing parameters of the I/NAV navigation message on E1-B, a component of the Galileo E1 signal, using previously reserved bits, so it costs no extra bandwidth ([EUSPA](https://www.euspa.europa.eu/galileo-osnma)). Receivers implement the protocol and download certified public keys from the European GNSS Service Centre. The EU Agency for the Space Programme declared OSNMA operational on 24 July 2025, after a public test phase from November 2021; it is mandatory for the new generation of EU smart tachographs ([announcement](https://www.euspa.europa.eu/newsroom-events/news/testing-operations-galileo-osnma-service-now-available-users)).

EUSPA says OSNMA makes signals "unpredictable and difficult to replay", and that a planned Signal Authentication Service will add "protection at pseudorange level". In other words, OSNMA today proves the navigation *data* came from Galileo; it does not yet prove the timing of the signal itself.

Authenticated navigation data is not the same as an authenticated measurement. Keep consistency checks running even with OSNMA, and do not let one GNSS source be the only clock for systems like base stations or substations.

Spoofing is caught by inconsistency: with physics, with your own clock's history, with other receivers and other time sources. Signing the navigation data (OSNMA) raises the bar, and a backup timing source keeps you running while you investigate.

blocks.question: In the detector's log, why does the speed check never fire even though the receiver is being spoofed?
options: The vehicle is parked
The spoofer keeps the position change small and smooth, inside the plausibility limit, while pulling the time
Speed checks only work for aircraft
The log has too few records
blocks.explain: DHS warns manipulation can produce ramping errors within expected bounds. A single plausibility check is easy to stay under; combining it with clock self-consistency catches what it misses.

blocks.question: What does Galileo OSNMA, as operational in 2025, authenticate?
options: The Galileo open-service navigation data (ephemeris and timing parameters), so receivers can verify it came from Galileo unmodified
Every receiver's position
The exact arrival time of every signal at pseudorange level
GPS signals only
blocks.explain: OSNMA signs I/NAV navigation data on E1-B. EUSPA says pseudorange-level protection will come from the planned Signal Authentication Service, and GPS L1 C/A data authentication is a future evolution.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a telecom and space defence map

blocks.md:
Every lesson found the same pattern: a system built for a small, trusted group was opened to many parties without adding checks on who may ask for what. SS7 trusted any Global Title; Diameter trusts a sender's own Origin-Realm; GSM trusted any mast; carriers trusted callers who knew a few personal details; an old Twitter feature trusted a phone number; KA-SAT's management network trusted anyone inside it; GEO links trusted that nobody listens; GNSS receivers trust any signal that looks right.

The fixes also rhyme: authenticate the peer and bind its claims to that authentication (SEPP, AKA, OSNMA); check that requests are plausible for the subject (signalling categories, trajectory checks, SIM-swap signals, clock consistency); encrypt every hop you do not control (satellite backhaul, null ciphers); and audit what systems actually do against what you approved (lawful interception, router configuration, fleet commands).

scenes.caption: Interconnect (lessons 2 to 5, 9): category filtering and SMS home routing for SS7, realm checks for Diameter, SEPP with N32 protection for 5G.
Radio and SIM (lessons 6 to 8, 10): mutual AKA, SUCI with a provisioned key, 2G and null ciphers disabled, OTA and binary SMS filtered, eSIM codes protected.
Customer identity (lesson 11): carrier authentication, locks and notifications before SIM changes and ports; relying parties check SIM-swap signals and move to passkeys.
Management and lawful interception (lessons 12, 13): out-of-band management, golden configs, AAA accounting, and audits of intercepts against warrants.
Satellite and timing (lessons 14 to 17): encrypt backhaul yourself and verify it; guard fleet commands; cross-check GNSS time and keep a backup clock.

blocks.md:
**Detection signals, by source:**

- *Signalling firewall and STP/HLR logs*: category 1 messages from outside, category 2 messages whose sender is not the IMSI's home, impossible travel in location updates, bursts of SendRoutingInfoForSM from one Global Title.
- *Diameter and SEPP logs*: realm or network ID that does not match the connection's peer, discarded N32 messages, rate-limit hits.
- *Radio network*: measurement reports showing unknown cells, unplanned channels or implausible signal strength.
- *Carrier CRM (customer relationship management) systems*: SIM changes and port-outs, failed authentication attempts, staff accessing accounts before authentication.
- *Router and LI systems*: configuration drift, AAA command accounting, on-box containers and captures, tunnels to unknown addresses, intercepts without warrants.
- *Satellite and PNT*: cleartext on your own captures; clock bias and drift disagreeing; several receivers losing lock at once.

**Practise legally.** Do not transmit on any radio band, send signalling to networks you do not operate, or capture other people's satellite traffic; those can need a licence or be illegal. Everything in this course runs on a laptop:
- Run and extend this course's code: add Diameter rules, a SEPP policy for more headers, more GNSS checks.
- Open the GSM MAP captures on the [Wireshark sample captures](https://wiki.wireshark.org/SampleCaptures) page, name each operation and check whether lesson 4's categories cover it.
- Read the specs you met, all free from ETSI: [TS 33.501](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133500_133599/133501/19.07.00_60/ts_133501v190700p.pdf), [TS 33.102](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133100_133199/133102/19.01.00_60/ts_133102v190100p.pdf) and [TS 33.127](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133100_133199/133127/19.08.00_60/ts_133127v190800p.pdf).
- Practise log analysis and incident response on [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) and general skills on [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/).

**Related courses.** The **Wireless and mobile security** course covers Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and phone platform security, and the **Social engineering, human factors and physical security** course covers carrier insiders and help-desk verification in depth.

Telecom and space systems fail in the same way: trust given to whoever can reach an interface. Bind every claim to an authenticated peer, check that requests make sense for their subject, encrypt hops you do not control, and audit what the system really does.

blocks.question: Which pair of controls addresses the same underlying problem in two generations of signalling?
options: SMS home routing and Galileo OSNMA
SUCI and router golden configs
Satellite IPsec and carrier account locks
SS7 category 2 filtering and the 5G SEPP's check of the originating network ID against the peer's certificate
blocks.explain: Both decide whether the sender may speak about this subscriber or network. Category 2 filtering compares the sender's GT with the IMSI's home; the SEPP compares the claimed network ID with what the authenticated peer's certificate represents, which closes the spoofing gap.

blocks.question: Your company relies on SMS one-time codes and a GEO satellite link to a remote site, and its masts use GNSS for timing. Which single principle from this course covers all three risks?
options: Buy more bandwidth
Move all servers to the cloud
Do not trust a channel you do not control without your own verification: phishing-resistant MFA, your own encryption on the link, and independent time checks
Turn off logging to reduce attack surface
blocks.explain: SMS depends on carriers and signalling, the satellite link is broadcast to a footprint, and GNSS signals can be spoofed. In each case you add verification you control: passkeys, IPsec or TLS, and clock consistency with a backup source.
